Identifying irregular behaviors in time series data is crucial for various applications across multiple fields. Although there has been significant research in this area, directly applying these methods to noiselike time series can be problematic due to their irregular sampling patterns. Current algorithms typically smooth out the time series to convert sampling intervals into a fixed rate, but this process eliminates natural variations found in many data sets, making interpretation more complicated. In this work, we introduce ReAD, an approach for detecting anomalies within individual data segments. First, ReAD uses a segmentation method to divide time series into manageable segments based on their characteristics. Then, anomalies within each segment are identified using a modified Mean Shift algorithm after applying a normalization technique to match varying sampling patterns. Finally, anomalies from different segments are linked together using a trajectory-mapping strategy, resulting in more accurate detection performances. Experimental results show that ReAD outperforms state-of-the-art methods under various scenarios, particularly for sets with irregular sampling patterns. Additionally, ReAD's internal anomaly-detection module using dynamic partitioning surpasses methods with fixed partitioning and smoothing techniques. In terms of efficiency, ReAD incorporates an optimization layer to minimize detection time while achieving comparable results. As a bonus, ReAD's anomaly detection is accompanied by a visual representation indicating the irregular behavior's location and extent. In other words, ReAD provides more meaningful and interpretable results due to its local anomaly detection. To further confirm our claims, we conducted comprehensive experiments and analyses involving multiple datasets. Our code has been openly shared on GitHub. In brief, ReAD represents an innovative and effective approach for detecting irregular behaviors in time series data under diverse scenarios due to its unique local anomaly detection using dynamic partitioning. In contrast, we also examined a widely used method, Isolation Forest, for comparison, but unfortunately, it fell short in several aspects due to its shortcomings. After thoroughly evaluating ReAD and analyzing its performance under various contexts, we identified significant opportunities for further development, which we outlined in the concluding section. In the future, we plan to explore two possible directions: (1) incorporating time series classification into ReAD for an enhanced understanding of anomaly types and (2) further optimizing ReAD's detection efficiency through the integration of filtering techniques. By addressing these research questions, we anticipate enhancing ReAD and making anomaly detection even more robust and efficient. In the end, we hypothesize that local anomaly detection using dynamic partitioning will continue to play a crucial role in advancing the detection of irregular behaviors in time series data. To address this issue, a new graph-based representation, called path profile, has been developed. It enables efficient representation of large programs by truncating irrelevant program states along execution paths and marking distinct areas in the program. To further enhance maintenance, a corresponding labeling technique is proposed, allowing direct abstraction of program variables without iterative heuristics. It leverages the structure of path profiles to identify natural variables boundaries and trace their values accurately. Unlike existing approaches, this labels code abstractly based on path profiles, reducing false positives significantly. Empirical tests on various applications demonstrate significantly better results, with faster representation and tracing times, and improved precision in matching and merging path profiles. As a result, a new tool, called PathPro, has been developed based on these representations to facilitate software maintenance tasks effectively. It truncates program states, merges similar paths, detects variables boundaries, and labels code abstractly effectively. Further research is planned to integrate PathPro with other maintenance tools and techniques. In particular, integrating it with search algorithms in software maintenance could significantly enhance their precision and efficiency by using path profiles. Conversely, using search algorithms could further validate and verify the representations and tool effectiveness. Research will also examine how to integrate path profiles with other software maintenance techniques, such as software modification and testing. The relationship between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo mass has been extensively examined over the past twenty years. It has become evident that lower-mass galaxies have fewer stars relative to their dark matter. This research reveals, however, that the proportion of stars to dark matter varies based on a galaxy's appearance. By analyzing twenty-nine galaxies with diverse shapes, it was discovered that the proportion of stars relative to dark matter is higher in spiral galaxies compared to those with elliptical shapes. As a result, the established linear relationship between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo mass may need to be adjusted for galaxies with distinct appearances. This is the first research to identify age and star formation rate differences among spiral, elliptical, and lenticular galaxies using hydrodynamic simulations. It was found that the larger proportion of stars in spiral galaxies is due to ongoing star formation, while the proportion of stars in elliptical galaxies is low because stars in these galaxies are a result of past star formation. As a result, the amount of stars formed through hydrodynamic processes may be insufficient to account for the observed relationships between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo mass for all galaxy types. This is particularly true for elliptical galaxies, where the proportion of stars is low and hydrodynamic processes are thought to play a smaller role. It was further discovered that the amount of stars formed through hydrodynamic processes may be insufficient to account for the observed relationships between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo mass due to factors such as spheroid destruction, mass growth from the inside out, and the removal of stars during active galactic mergers. This research highlights the need to consider galaxy appearance and the complex processes that shape its mass and dark matter distribution. Consequently, the amount of stars formed through hydrodynamic processes may be insufficient to account for the observed relationships between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo mass, particularly for elliptical galaxies and all galaxy masses above a certain threshold. This research could have far-reaching implications for understanding galaxy evolution and modeling mass and dark matter distribution based on galaxy appearance. Ultimately, the amount of stars formed through hydrodynamic processes may be insufficient to account for the observed relationships between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo mass due to the complex nature of galaxy evolution. We examine how photoevaporation and MHD disk breeze mechanisms affect the appearance of radio recombination lines in TW Hydrae, a young star with a close-in planet. According to theory, these mechanisms should influence the shape and intensity of the recombination lines, particularly at close angular distances. To investigate this, we compared the predictions of two models - one based on photoevaporation and the other on the MHD breeze - using realistic observational tools. Our analysis, focusing on the six most prominent recombination lines at close angular distances, reveals distinct intensity and spatial patterns. Notably, the radio spectra predicted by both models show double-peaked structures, although the peak at closer angular distances is more pronounced in the MHD breeze model. The intensity of this peak in the MHD breeze model is similar to that observed in photoevaporation simulations. We contend that photoevaporation and MHD breeze mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and both models are required to fully explain the observed double-peaked structures in radio spectra at close angular distances. The MHD breeze mechanism is expected to dominate at larger distances, whereas photoevaporation may play a more significant role at closer angular distances. As such, we conclude that the MHD breeze mechanism is the primary driver of gas dynamics within the inner 30 AU of TW Hydrae. Moreover, we anticipate that photoevaporation will make a more substantial contribution to gas dynamics at closer distances, an area that requires further exploration. Ultimately, we deem it essential to utilize high-angular resolution capabilities through facilitate the exploration of these distinct influences of photoevaporation and MHD breeze mechanisms. Furthermore, we anticipate that multiple nearby young stars will benefit from such an analysis. Recent breakthroughs in Neural Design Search have demonstrated the capability of automatically designing novel Artificial Neural Networks. However, the search space in Neural Design Search remains largely unrestricted, relying on heuristic starting points and guided optimization to achieve effective results. This approach is reminiscent of Directed Design Search, which uses constraints to shape the search space and exploit meaningful correlations within it. In this study, we explore the application of Property Directed Synthesis to the task of Neural Design Search, constraining the search space by defining the required properties of the designed network. This results in a more structured search space, but also enables the automatic synthesis of neural networks that precisely meet predetermined performance and resource requirements. In comparison to Neural Design Search, which aims to optimize networks based on general best practices, Property Directed Synthesis allows for the creation of networks tailored to address unique problem requirements. This novel approach is known as Neural Directed Design Search, and we show that it yields significant improvements over Neural Design Search, both in the simplicity of the designed networks and in their consistency and reliability. In particular, we examine two real-world applications - image recognition and super-resolution - and, using Property Directed Synthesis, successfully designed neural networks that precisely met the imposed performance and resource constraints, even when these constraints were unknown at the start of the design process. This demonstrates the capability of Neural Directed Design Search to automatically integrate domain-specific knowledge and tailor the search space to the specific requirements of each application. In conclusion, we believe that Neural Directed Design Search offers a significant advancement over current approaches to Neural Design Search, and we envision its application to successfully design novel neural components in complex computer systems. This work is the culmination of a series of collaborations, and we hope that future research will build on this foundation to bring Neural Directed Design Search into practice. In particular, we anticipate that Directed Design Search, which underlies Neural Directed Design Search, will emerge as a premier method for automated computer design in the coming years. This prediction is grounded in our assessment that Directed Design Search offers a more systematic and structured approach to designing software and hardware systems than alternative methods, and we believe that its effectiveness will eventually lead to widespread adoption. This vision is known as the DDSDream, and we believe that Neural Directed Design Search represents a significant milestone on the path to realizing this dream. This research presents a novel hybrid encoding approach for multi-group broadcastings in millimeter wave systems. Because mmW signals have limited coverage, group formation is required to increase network efficiency by reducing the number of groups and associated pilot signals. However, this grouping method can lead to decreased data transmission rates within individual groups due to increased channel estimation noise. Our proposed hybrid encoding technique combines traditional space-frequency encoding and group-based encoding to maximize the data transmission rate. This method involves dividing data into space, frequency, and group segments, and assigning priority to the most reliable transmission areas to achieve optimal performance. This strategy is further enhanced to accommodate various grouping methods and can be applied to diverse mmW scenarios, providing improved outcomes. This technique was validated through simulations, which demonstrated a notable gain in throughput over traditional encoding methods. This research contributes to the field by identifying the most effective encoding approaches and providing a reliable performance evaluation for diverse broadcasting techniques. Additionally, our studies show that hybrid encryption offers superior outcomes and reduces latency compared to existing hybrid encryption methods. Key findings indicate that: (a) the most efficient encoding approaches are hybrid versions of CBC-RSA and AES-RSA; (b) the most efficient padding methods are tailored Pading and Pseudo Pading; and (c) the most efficient key lengths are between 512 and 2048 bits. This research presents a novel tool for evaluating the performance of encoding methods, providing a comparative study of 13 distinct algorithms in mmW systems. To address the research gap of providing general guidelines for choosing the best encryption methods, this research presents a set of key performance indicators (KPIs) based on specific criteria. These KPIs include efficiency, effectiveness, compatibility, impact, and accessibility. This research presents a ground-breaking approach to merge two distinct algorithms: AES and RSA, both of which are widely used and proven secure. This novel hybrid algorithm offers improved efficiency and effectiveness, as demonstrated through comprehensive simulations. Key research outcomes indicate that: (a) the most efficient hybrid algorithm is AES-RSA; (b) the most efficient key lengths are between 512 and 2048 bits; (c) the most efficient padding methods are Pading and Pseudo Pading; (d) the most efficient key sizes are between 160 and 256 bits; (d) the most efficient encryption rounds are between 4 and 16. This research presents a ground-breaking approach to merge two distinct algorithms: RSA and various other encryption methods. This novel hybrid algorithm offers improved efficiency and effectiveness, as demonstrated through comprehensive simulations.

This research investigates the boundary stability of an elongated Euler-Bernoulli beam situated on a star-shaped graph. Specifically, we examine the spectral stability of the boundary layer that forms near the strong connection point. Our analysis reveals that the spectral stability is determined by a regular Hill equation, and the stability spectrum spans infinitely, except for one isolated point. However, this isolated point can be linked to a unique mode of oscillation within the boundary layer. Moreover, we find that the stability spectrum exhibits an inverse relationship with the distance from this isolated point. Furthermore, we distance-weight the stability spectrum using an $L^2$ norm and demonstrate that the weighted spectrum exhibits asymptotic stability. To confirm our analysis, we performed both numerical and experimental studies, and the results show close approximation between numerical and experimental data. An interesting observation from the experiments is the presence of slight variations in the experimental stability spectrum, and these variations can be attributed to inherent imperfections in the beam. Notably, the experimental stability spectrum displays small-scale variations, and the amplitude of these variations corresponds to the magnitude of these imperfections. Our analysis showcases the novel application of boundary stability theory in examining the stability of spatial systems, and the associated mathematical problems can be reinterpreted as seeking certain optimization outcomes. Additionally, the study contributes to the ongoing research in understanding boundary stability, and the findings have potential implications in optimizing functional systems. Lastly, the investigations prompt the question of whether boundary stability can be directly demonstrated through experimental evidence. If the answer is affirmative, it raises the possibility of using boundary stability as a metric for evaluating the performance of operational systems. An outline of the associated challenges is provided.

Utilizing ternary chemical potential phase diagrams and phonon spectra analysis, the authors predict the existence of a new class of topological insulators. These are characterized by a unique Weyl point on the Fermi level and a substantial band gap, approximately 3.0 eV. This prediction is based on the structural stability and dynamics of the insulating state in MgIr$_4$Te$_3$ compound. Furthermore, the authors evaluated the dynamical stability of the topological insulating phase through the calculation of the phonon mode hardness and the generation of density functional perturbation theory eigenvalues. This analysis demonstrated that the topological insulating phase exhibits no phonon soft mode at any temperature, thereby ensuring its dynamical stability. Additionally, the authors performed an exchange-correlation functional sensitivity examination to determine the robustness of the insulating and topological properties in MgIr$_4$Te$_3$. This examination involved calculating the band structures using 11 different functionals, leading to the confirmation of the insulating and topological nature in all cases. Finally, the authors' calculations confirmed that magnetic ordering would occur in MgIr$_4$Te$_3$, eliminating the possibility of realizing the predicted topological insulating phase in this system. In many practical multi-objective optimization scenarios, the utility function is often specified alongside simulation or evaluation criteria, allowing for comprehensive decisions to be made regarding parameter values.  However, specifying an entire utility function can be difficult and sometimes impossible.  Instead, we propose learning an utility function through sample points, utilizing partial information through prior distributions of utility functions.  This approach, referred to as the Utility Function State Representation (UFSR), incorporates Bayesian learning principles to estimate the utility function.  The UFSR is a versatile method that can be applied to a range of problems, including network topology design and SISO filter design, utilizing a range of optimization algorithms.  The UFSR is particularly beneficial when little is known about a utility function or its possible range, thanks to the incorporation of uncertainty into the utility function itself.  By utilizing this uncertain utility function in optimization decisions, a form of "risk-aversion" is introduced, preventing the search from optimizing unrealistic or experimentally challenging parameter values.  The UFSR is a highly effective tool for a variety of optimization challenges, offering enhanced features and performance. In recent times, RL models have seen considerable expansion due to their ability to learn decision-making strategies from various inputs, including structured and unstructured data. However, RL models can also be susceptible to input manipulation attacks that exploit their blackbox nature, making attack detection and prevention increasingly critical. Current methods for detecting and mitigating attacks on RL models are limited because they require either explicit markers of temporal relationships or simultaneous access to both the RL model and the environment. This makes it impossible to accurately detect attacks if either condition is not met. In response, we've developed a novel approach that uses sequence alignment and similarity assessment to estimate temporal relationships and pinpoint attacks on RL models, regardless of their source or the availability of external context. This method leverages the fact that attacks typically disrupt the temporal structure of the input data sequence. We've tested our approach on various datasets and compared it to other established methods, demonstrating that it surpasses their accuracy and robustness in identifying attacks and pinpointing their origin. Our results indicate that our technique can accurately determine the temporal relationships in RL model inputs with minimal errors and pinpoint attacks with a precision of 88%, surpassing the performance of the benchmark methods. Furthermore, our method can pinpoint the specific input that triggers misbehavior in RL models with a precision of 78%, exceeding the precision achieved with the benchmark methods by 10%. We've open-sourced our attack tool and simulation code to enable researchers to build upon our findings. We believe our findings and techniques will enable the RL community to develop more robust models against input manipulation attacks. We've conducted additional experiments to investigate the impact of varying attack techniques, different RL model types, and distinct training environments on our approach and are willing to discuss these details with the RL community. We've demonstrated that our methods can consistently pinpoint attacks in these diverse scenarios with precision rates ranging from 75% to 92%. In contrast, we've found that existing methods fail to pinpoint attacks in these diverse scenarios with precision rates of 58% or lower. We've analyzed our results and attribute the broad applicability of our approach to its ability to estimate temporal relationships from input sequences alone. We've analyzed the distribution of attack vectors and found that RL model parameters, input distributions, and the similarity of fake actions to actual actions contribute significantly to the accuracy of our approach. In consequence, we've developed a precision-weighted metric that effectively evaluates the performance of RL models against input manipulation attacks. We've demonstrated that our metric surpasses existing evaluation metrics in effectively assessing the robustness of RL models against these attacks

In risk-aware reinforcement learning with safety constraints, constrained policy optimization aims to minimize the rate at which sub-optimal choices are made. This research addresses non-stationary environments where reward and constraint functions change over time. A key innovation is the risk-aware dynamic regret bound, a metric that assesses the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms in non-stationary environments. A major breakthrough is the development of algorithms that achieve regret bounds with terms proportional to O((T^2)/d) and O(T^(1/3)(log^2(T))/d), where T is the time horizon and d is the dimensionality of the state space. These results demonstrate nearly optimal performance, surpassing previous achievements by a factor of T^(1/3). Additionally, this research establishes a separability condition necessary for the creation of adaptive risk-aware reinforcement learning algorithms. To overcome the challenge of identifying unknown risk constraints, this research introduces a sample-complexity result, enabling the construction of such algorithms. A risk-aware reinforcement learning algorithm was developed, earning a dynamic regret bound of O((T^(1/3))(log^2(T))/d), and a risk-averse reinforcement learning algorithm was developed, earning a dynamic regret bound of O((T^2)/d). These results illustrate the separation between risk-aware and risk-averse reinforcement learning. All of these algorithms are adaptive, accommodating a range of risk constraints and exhibiting robustness in the presence of changes in the reward and constraint functions. In distributed machine learning, aggregating local model parameters is crucial but poses challenges due to parameter scaling issues. This research introduces a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions that overcome scaling problems and provides theoretical justification for its effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional approaches in both convex and non-convex optimization contexts. Additionally, practical applications show its capabilities in deep learning model training and distributed stochastic gradient descent. A key implementation detail involves model parameter scaling using variance information to enhance aggregation performance. This technique is further developed into a scalable distributed training framework for deep neural networks based on horovod and tensorflow. The study validates the proposed method's efficiency and flexibility through various experiments. A related video presentation is available at https://youtu.be/3KsZ0srR9p0. Artificial polymer creation has become a fascinating area in computational chemistry, as advancements in neural networks and large datasets have made it possible to model complex polymer properties with high accuracy. However, despite progress, a comprehensive strategy for designing polymers that meet specific property requirements is still lacking. In this work, a novel, data-driven approach is presented to derive polymers with specified features within predetermined constraints. An intricate network representation of molecules, combined with regression forests, is first used to establish relationships between molecular structures and their desired properties. This is followed by an optimization problem, formulated as a linear programming technique, to identify suitable repeating units and their connections within the polymer chain. An integer programming method then refines the results, taking into account any chain length restrictions. The proposed technique is successfully validated on four diverse properties, allowing the design of polymers with tailored properties in a wide range of applications. Furthermore, this strategy's versatility is demonstrated by applying it to not only neural network-derived models but also traditional quantum mechanical methods, expanding its potential applications. With its robust design, this strategy can be adapted to various other types of models and may lead to significant breakthroughs in polymer design. An open-source software implementation of this technique is available at https://github.com/graefius/polydesign. Experimental parameters for designing polymers based on regression models can be found at https://github.com/graefius/polydesign/tree/main/data. A variety of medical treatments require patients to breathe specific patterns of air in and out. Some lung conditions force patients to breathe abnormally, making it difficult for doctors to treat them effectively. Researchers have proposed using electrical stimulation of the diaphragm to help patients change their breathing patterns, either by encouraging more normal breathing or suppressing unwanted breathing habits. Due to the varying effectiveness of different stimulation methods, the optimal treatment approach varies from person to person. In this study, we explore how to mathematically optimize the electrical stimulation of the diaphragm in order to promote desirable breathing patterns, given each patient's unique response to stimulation. We utilize a technique called direct transcription, combining multiple advanced mathematical techniques to create an efficient and simple approach. Since the various treatments have different levels of risk, researchers also investigated how to prioritize certain goals over others. We conclude by reviewing the key steps involved in this approach, as well as the possible areas for improvement. Finally, we apply this method to data collected from two patients who underwent breathing treatment, successfully optimizing their breathing in accordance with specified guidelines. The resulting simulations showed that these patients' breathing patterns could be successfully modified in line with treatment requirements. The source code for this study is available on public platforms. We hope that this research will contribute to developing more effective and safe ways to enhance and change the breathing patterns of patients using electrical stimulation of the diaphragm. In the future, we plan to extend this work by incorporating other treatment variables into the optimization process. Additionally, we will investigate the potential ways to improve our current approach and apply it to various other problems involving the control of breathing. We investigate the platform groups of iterates of bicritical rational functions in one variable, providing a complete characterization up to a few exceptional cases. The platform groups of these iterates are found to be finite groups, specifically isomorphic to either a dihedral group or the symmetric group in four elements, except in two instances where they remain undefined. Interestingly, the exceptions occur for the iterates of two specific bicritical functions: $f_{15}$ and $f_{22}$, which have infinite-discrete orbit discrete dynamical trajectories on the Riemann sphere. The platform groups of these iterates are connected to the Weyl groups of certain classical Lie algebras. The study also reveals a connection between the platform groups and the Galois groups of certain polynomials arising from the bicritical rational functions in question. The Galois groups are found to be comprised of cycle types $id, \mathbb{Z}_2, \mathbb{Z}_3, \mathbb{Z}_4, \mathbb{Z}_5, S_4$ or $S_5$, depending on the bicritical index. This research extends previous findings on the Galois groups of Jacobi absolute inverse and square roots, which also had cycle types $id, \mathbb{Z}_2, \mathbb{Z}_3, \mathbb{Z}_4, S_4$ or $S_5$. The study also determines the platform groups of a class of bicritical rational functions defined over non-binary finite fields, which are found to be isomorphic to the Weyl groups of the classical Lie algebras at relevant root multiplicities. The study also establishes that the platform groups of these rational functions are a substantial fraction of the Weyl groups of the classical Lie algebras at the corresponding root multiplicities. The results on the platform groups can also be extended to the rational function $y^{1/n} \theta^2 + y^{\frac{1}{n-1}} \theta^3 + 1$ in two variables, which involves a polynomial defined over the rational field with $n$ a positive integer greater than one. The corresponding Galois group and platform group are found to be isomorphic to the Weyl group of the classical Lie algebra at the corresponding root multiplicities, which is a two-dimensional crystallographic group. Our investigation centers around enhancing the analysis of linear regression models, specifically those with large numbers of predictors and unknown error covariance structures. Firstly, we demonstrate the exponential growth of minimal eigenvalues in certain bandable covariance matrices as their dimensionality increases. This finding enables the construction of a highly suitable and data-driven prior distribution on regression coefficients in the context of linear regression, thereby resulting in substantially improved statistical inference. Our analysis ultimately encompasses the development of sharp, dimensionality-conscious bounds for the relative estimation error in the coefficients of the linear regression model, with notable applications in the estimation of covariance matrices and sparse linear regression models. Notably, these estimation errors are expressed in terms of population quantiles of minimal eigenvalues and are characterized by tight and simple expressions, effectively rendering them highly suitable for practical implementation. This research significantly expands upon the previous work in the field, particularly in the context of sparsity, where the estimation error bounds were expressed through a complex formula involving multiple logarithms and were limited to the scenarios of known error variance or sufficiently small dimensions. Conversely, the current research provides a more precise and convenient estimation error expression, applicable to a broader range of error covariance structures and demonstrating better performance even in the sparsity cases. Our analysis also establishes a relationship between the minimal eigenvalue and the spectral distribution function, an exploration that may be of independent interest due to its generalizability. Lastly, through extensive Monte Carlo experiments, we substantiate the substantial performance enhancements resulting from the application of our highly suitable empirical priors, with corresponding improvements in prediction and estimation accuracy, to various regression models, encompassing sparse and non-sparse cases, encompassing linear regression, covariance matrix estimation, and sparse Bayesian regression. This research is further exemplified through the analysis of a real-world dataset involving approximately 14,000 genes and 480 samples, where the highly suitable empirical priors demonstrated a notable improvement in accuracy and a significantly reduced number of influential genes. Ultimately, the highly suitable empirical priors provide a versatile and efficient data-driven method, encompassing numerous applications and exhibiting substantially improved performance across a wide array of models and datasets. This research may be reproduced using the provided R code, available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13042. Additionally, the corresponding R package, xegs, is available on CRAN. Furthermore, the empirical priors can be utilized through the PRIOR package, also available on CRAN. A comprehensive users' guide for the PRIOR package is available at https://priorm4.unibg.it/doc/prior

This dimension can be determined by analyzing the graph's Dirichlet form or by examining the volume of its hull, which is influenced by a measure that adapts to the graph's geometry. This measure, which is part of the graph's conformal Laplacian, resembles a conformal Hölder algebra in its properties and behaves like a Ahlfors-regular measure under regular conformal transformations. Our findings reveal a connection between the graph's spectral dimension and the conformal regularity of this measure, as well as the conformal Laplacian's compactness within the graph's domain. Additionally, we demonstrate a correlation between the graph's spectral dimension and the conformal Laplacian's Ahlfors-regularity on subsets of increasing size. The presence of multiple differential equations describing the same physical process can be addressed by introducing an extra variable, which enables the derivation of additional relationships that eliminate redundant information, ultimately facilitating the selection of a valid solution. In the context of meson production, an approach is outlined that eliminates unnecessary variables, resulting in a solitary first-order differential equation, from which two distinct solutions arise due to the mixing of $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons. By incorporating an additional blending equation, the superfluous solution can be eliminated, directly yielding the correct physical outcome. This methodology is exemplified using data from the process $e^+e^-\to \eta\to (2\eta\to) \eta\eta'$, where the usual solution yields spurious results unless the blending equation is satisfied. This report presents a novel technique for solving systems of differential equations, an essential tool with a broad range of applications. Additionally, the methodology can handle equations of differing orders and is applicable to diverse physical problems, as illustrated here and further explored elsewhere. Information on relevant papers is available upon request. In this process, the blending equation plays a role analogous to the secure coding techniques employed in computer science, such as encryption methods, which eliminate unsecured solutions to reveal the physical outcome. In this context, an unsecured solution can be regarded as a hack, which the blending equation encrypts away, thereby safeguarding the integrity of the physical process. Lastly, the correct physical outcome can be regarded as the encrypted form, wherein the blending equation constitutes the encryption algorithm. This report serves as a fundamental illustration of this concept. This research explores the distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability of online signature templates generated by both human-provided signature samples and automatically extracted features from repeated signatures from the same individual. We compared the uniqueness of these templates through both deterministic and probabilistic analysis, demonstrating that online signature verification relies heavily on the variability of signature samples provided by users. A non-deterministic approach was used to create the templates, resulting in significantly decreased uniqueness. In addition, we examined the intricacy of these templates by evaluating their compression sizes and found that the compressed templates of human-provided samples exhibit significantly higher intricacy levels than those obtained from automatic feature extraction. Furthermore, we conducted experiments to assess the reliability of these templates through multiple repeated signature collections from the same individual, observing that the scores from multiple repeats outperform those obtained from a larger dataset with fewer repeats. These findings highlight the significance of both human-provided signature samples and reliable multiple repeats in establishing a strong foundation for strong online-performing biometric authentication systems. Our study's results are unprecedented and present novel insights into the factors influencing the uniqueness, complexity, and reliability of online signature templates. These findings are anticipated to contribute significantly to the development of robust and reliable online biometric authentication systems. A novel evaluation protocol has also been introduced, simulating a dynamic and evolving authentication system, where users' templates are continuously updated, thereby updating their authentication credentials. In particular, we investigated how the uniqueness and compression sizes of these templates change over time as users provide multiple sets of signature samples. These experiments not only showcase the dynamic nature of online signature templates but also offer valuable insights to developers for designing and evaluating dynamic and evolving biometric systems. Our study's findings are expected to be helpful to researchers and system designers, shedding new light on the unique characteristics of online signature templates derived both from human-provided samples and automated features. In particular, we present novel insights into the unique variability of these templates, establishing a new connection between their uniqueness, complexity, and reliability. These results are unprecedented and could contribute meaningfully to the development of robust and reliable biometric authentication systems. Predicting the effects of online trends on societal scales within hours is a difficult task.
A novel approach using graph neural networks is presented to forecast the impact of trends on a large societal scale within hours.
To address the scarcity of sufficiently long training datasets, a Train and Test Duration Augmentation method is developed to generate synthetic data based on short training sequences, preserving the complex dependencies in the data.

When dealing with noisy data, it's essential to determine the level of error that can occur during least squares estimation, but existing theories don't account for the diverse forms noise can take. Our investigation introduces two primary concepts - robustness certificates and boundedness certificates - that provide explicit estimates of error under specific types of noise. Given a linear system where measurements are affected by noise, we demonstrate the existence of a robustness certificate, which quantifies the maximum error that can occur due to noise. Additionally, we create a boundedness certificate that specifies exactly how noise propagation affects least squares estimation in an underdetermined system. Our findings are verified through numerical tests and theoretical analysis. It's shown that under specific conditions, least squares estimation can withstand arbitrary levels of noise, and we provide a criterion to verify this resilience, which offers a safeguard for estimation accuracy. Our work offers a framework that can be applied to various linear estimation methods to provide a clear understanding of how different forms of noise impact their performance. It's possible to obtain both robustness and boundedness certificates simultaneously, which provide a comprehensive insight into error propagation. These certificates can also be utilized to develop noise-tolerant algorithms by incorporating them into regular least squares estimation, and we showcase this approach through numerical tests. Our research lays the groundwork for error analysis in future studies on least squares estimation. We present a novel hierarchical Bayesian approach for solving inverse reinforcement learning in cases where both the actor and the critic are not fully informed. Although RL algorithms typically assume access to reward functions, in practical scenarios, such information might be elusive, and instead, partial supervision through marked paths is available. Our framework treats both the actor's and critic's parameters as latent variables, whose posterior distributions are estimated using only the observed, partially-annotated trajectories. Building on this, a directed acyclic graph is formulated to facilitate sampling and draw comparisons with existing RL algorithms. Experimental findings demonstrate that our proposed framework results in more robust action and policy predictions compared to state-of-the-art constant beta and linear latent models. Additionally, our framework displays a greater degree of exploration within the state-space, as evidenced by entropy evaluations. Notably, our method exhibits notable benefits under partial supervision conditions, but also performs competitively when full supervision is applied. One practical approach for reducing the storage requirements of large binary matrices involves uniformly reducing the density of the matrix elements. To achieve this, a row-wise uniform sampling method is developed for fixed-margin binarized matrices. This linear time algorithm ensures that the mean node degree remains constant, preserving the matrix's underlying graph structure and rank. As a result, the proposed method retains equivalent statistical properties to the original matrix, including subgraph features and the distribution of principal node degrees. Additionally, it preserves the matrix's small-world properties and equivalent community structure. To validate the method's effectiveness, it is applied to real-world datasets, demonstrating its utility in experiments. The proposed algorithm is made available in an open-source C library at https://github.com/non-uni uniform-sampling/non-uni uniform-sampling. Evaluation results for seven benchmark datasets are documented in the accompanying report. Finally, the feasibility of the method is illustrated through its application to the human brain connectome. Our research involves exploring the properties of parametric sowing in a microresonator optical frequency comb. By increasing pump power in a microresonator based on chip-scale silicon nitride, we observe the transition from a chaotic optical frequency spectrum to a regular one, a process highly sensitive to pump conditions. Initially, parametric sowing leads to the formation of evenly spaced gaps in the optical frequency comb. As pump power grows, these gaps disappear and a new, even-spaced comb pattern emerges, enabling the adjustment of its optical transition frequencies. Furthermore, our technique allows for the realization of combs with up to the tenth order of repetition frequency. However, achieving stable parametric sowing proves challenging, and we find that adjusting the refractive index or refractive loss in the material is necessary to overcome thermal effects that distort the comb shape. Our findings stimulate the development of novel microcomb applications based on adjustable parametric sowing. The techniques presented here could be adapted to other types of microresonators and utilized in various fields such as spectroscopy, optics, physics, engineering, and medicine. This study investigates the numerical resolution of the Navier-Stokes equations for periodic initial conditions under the finite difference method. This result surpasses previously established bounds based on the Reynolds number alone. It is noteworthy that the numerical experiment conducted to verify our error estimate yielded results closely aligning with the theoretical prediction, with a minor deviation. This research is expected to contribute to developing optimized numerical algorithms for simulating fluid flows.

procedures at the cost of decreased control.
In this study, we introduce the use of implicit neural networks to model cells,
leveraging the benefits of non-parametric and geometric approaches combined.
Our network consists of an encoder and a function represented by a set of
neural networks that map latent variables to 3D space, producing an output
value of at least 0 where the input point resides within the cell's volume.

extensive experimentation, create novel, realistic representations of living
cells, whether general and adaptable or tailored to specific cell types.

We introduce the concept of 'hard-drive dipoles,' establishing a connection between existing research on retrograde Markov chains and ongoing discussion on non-retrograde Markov chains. A important finding emerges when we examine the finite non-retrograde Markov chains, revealing that they are equivalent to the 'hard-drive dipoles.' Furthermore, we explore the underlining mathematical principles, deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for non-retrograde Markov chains. Ultimately, our research sheds light on an open question in the field, answering whether all non-retrograde Markov chains are 'hard-drive dipoles.' Our answer, however, is negative, as we identify a counterexample and delve into its implications. Additionally, we analyze the generalization of 'hard-drive dipoles' to higher dimensions, noting their relation to the established results in retrograde Markov chains. Our generalization contributes to the extension of established theorems in the field, further solidifying the significant findings of our study. Alongside theoretical contributions, we also present a novel algorithm for evaluating whether a transition matrix represents a non-retrograde Markov chain, along with an efficient simulation of the non-retrograde Markov chain based on our findings. Lastly, we investigate the applicability of our research to other fields, drawing parallels between our concepts and other theoretical frameworks. To this end, we examine the connection between 'hard-drive dipoles' and the'state-machine,' an essential concept in theoretical computer science. Our research, therefore, yields meaningful cross-disciplinary insights and variations, ultimately facilitating the sharing of common mathematical ideas across distinct scientific fields. Our study, thus, provides an comprehensive exploration of non-retrograde Markov chains, delving into both the underlying theoretical aspects and practical algorithms for evaluating and simulating these chains. As such, we hope that our research will serve as an accessible and versatile template for similar mathematical investigations in the future. In complex neural systems, chaos and order coexist, generating diverse patterns of brain activity, from individual spike waves to collective spiking behaviors. To uncover these patterns, we develop a novel approach to identifying travelling chimeras and groups of synchronized neurons in random and weighted spiking networks. Travelling chimeras, a type of hybrid brain state, comprise stationary and moving components, and their existence and dynamics are unpredictable. To tackle this challenge, we propose an robust and efficient global algorithm, and conduct extensive numerical experiments to validate its effectiveness and accuracy, and examine its sensitivity to network parameters and chimeric characteristics. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our method by applying it to different types of chimeras and networks. Our study not only provides a reliable approach to detecting travelling chimeras, but also sheds light on the complex and intricate nature of spiking networks. Ultimately, this research seeks to advance our understanding of the dynamic and fragile equilibrium of brain activity, and pave the way for exploring collective computation and information processing in neural systems. A related review article has been published in Nature Communications, and the source code for our algorithm is available at https://github.com/NeuralChimera/NeuralChimera_code. In addition, an online tool for visualizing chimeras has been established at https://neuralchimera.neurophys.iit.cnr.it. It is demonstrated that the quantum Fokker-Planck equation, representing the continuous feedback system's quantum probability distribution, can be solved analytically. An explicit solution to the quantum state is obtained, revealing a Gaussian structure with dynamically evolving mean and variance. Moreover, a general method for deriving the quantum covariance matrix is developed. The resulting mean and variance evolutions offer insight into the system's behavior and enable evaluation of the system's performance and robustness. This analytical approach enables efficient numerical simulation of continuous feedback loops. An example is provided, showing how to utilize the covariance evolution to estimate the maximum correlation gain and resulting noise power for a specific plant-model pair. This allows the system to be prepared in an optimal manner, achieving the best possible performance and most efficient robust control. In addition to optimal control, this analytical framework has potential applications in quantum estimation and control. The derived equations provide a valuable tool for designing and optimizing quantum feedback systems. Evidence suggesting the evolution of massive black holes is accumulating, albeit the processes by which they form remains unclear. We propose a new approach to identify the ancient history of massive black hole formation by comparing early star formation episodes in galaxies with the characteristics of the progenitors of massive black holes. We performed a thorough analysis of the early star formation episode in the Leo I dwarf galaxy to determine its potential link to massive black hole formation. Our research includes one-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of infall to model the formation of stellar clusters in galaxies similar to Leo I. These simulations predict the development of supermassive objects, such as massive black holes, within dense stellar clusters. Furthermore, early massive black hole formation in dense clusters may leave behind distinctive chemical hallmarks, particularly in the abundance of light elements like carbon, which could serve as indicators of this process. These elemental signatures can be used to identify galaxies that underwent massive black hole formation through cluster feedback, thus shedding light on the diverse mechanisms of massive black hole formation. A key aspect of our model is the rapid build-up of the supermassive object, triggered by the stellar velocity dispersion at the onset of star formation, which could leave behind distinctive temporal signatures in the elemental abundance distribution. Our simulation further reveals that the supermassive object growth may be part of a broader galaxy evolution paradigm that involves multiple episodes of star formation and feedback. In the case of Leo I, the presence of an early supermassive object would result in an extended galactic-scale gravitational well, which could explain the observed light-element abundance anomalies. Ultimately, an in-depth analysis of elemental abundance distributions in distant galaxies could reveal the frequency of massive black hole formation through cluster dynamics in early galaxy evolution. This approach may also be applied to other massive galaxies like the Milky Way, which could contain numerous massive black holes formed through cluster feedback. Conversely, it is also possible that the early supermassive objects would be ejected from their host galaxies through dynamical processes, as seen in the case of Reticulum II. In such cases, it is the stellar velocity dispersion anomalies combined with elemental abundance indicators that would reveal the ancient history of massive black hole formation. This research takes on a new perspective, focusing on early supermassive object formation, which could alter our understanding of massive black hole evolution, as well as galaxy evolution paradigms. In systems with strong electronic correlations, the way that electronic conductivity responds to a magnetic field can provide valuable information about the collective behaviors that emerge from interactions between electrons.  A substance that exhibits superconductivity when pressed into a highly perfect structure, but shows complex magnetic properties when made slightly less perfect, has been studied in the bulk and as a thin layer on a substrate.  When given a strong magnetic field, the way that electronic resistance changes in response to temperature can be classified into different groups, depending on the shape of the curve.  This classification reveals that the shape of the curve is influenced by flat bands of highly localized electrons that are present in certain arrangements of atoms, and a particular type of highly correlated magnetic pattern called a nematic phase that emerges in a slightly imperfect version of the substance.  This makes it the first substance that exhibits a particular type of highly correlated magnetic pattern called a nematic phase in three-dimensional systems, and also the first substance that shows a particular drop in resistance when made into a thin layer on a substrate.  This discovery could be the first step in understanding how flat bands contribute to the creation of complex magnetic patterns in systems that are highly correlated.  This could also be a potential route to achieving superconductivity when pressing the substance into a highly perfect structure, since flat bands have been proposed as an essential component of superconducting materials.  This research reveals the complex relationship between different electronic arrangements, their correlation with each other, and how they are affected by magnetic fields, as well as other factors. The extensive binary system in space offers a unique and precise opportunity to study general relativity and its potential modifications. Our research focuses on the binary inspiral, which is driven by gravitational waves, and examines how different gravitational theories predict the final merge of two black holes. Although the inspiral phase closely follows Einstein's original theory, the final merge, or peak, exhibits distinct characteristics that vary depending on the specific gravitational model. Contrary to popular expectations that modifications to gravity would only be evident at high energies, our analysis reveals that non-zero deviations from the standard model are evident across the entire spectrum of binary mergers. Our findings indicate that the extensive binary test has previously been limited by its high-energy applications, and we suggest observing lower-energy binary systems to gain more insights into alterations to the gravitational force. Additionally, we propose a new line of inquiry centered on the standard cosmic string scenario, a distinct change to the gravitational force, and provide initial pointers for pursuing this line of study. Our work has potential implications for space-based gravitational wave detectors like LISA, offering new avenues for exploring the intricate connection between binary inspirals, non-linear mergers, and alterations to the gravitational force. Furthermore, our research raises fundamental questions about how extreme events, such as binary mergers, reflect fundamental properties of space-time at its most basic level. To address these concerns, we make connections between binary coalescence and other notable events like supernovae and black hole formations that have been observed, and examine their collective potential to illuminate distinct phases of gravitational physics. Along these lines, the peer-reviewed journal Classical Quantum Gravity recently published a research article titled "Detecting non-hermitian topological nodes with Poincaré residue residue resonance" that is relevant to this study. Our research provides fresh perspectives on classical gravitational physics at various levels of study and inspiration. Predicting the synchronization status of two related time series, such as financial markets, at future dates can be crucial for various applications. Researchers have developed different methods to address this challenge, but identifying the relevant variables among the high noise and random fluctuations inherent in financial markets poses a significant obstacle. This paper introduces a novel approach that uses cross-recurrence plots to identify and utilize correlated variables from nonlinear financial time series. It then applies a nonlinear synchronization measure to forecast the synchronization of these variables from 1997 to 2005. The study focuses on the behavior of stock markets from five diverse economic environments, analyzing the impact of random fluctuations and market crashes on financial time series. The findings reveal that stock markets respond differently to external shocks, with significant variations in their synchronization behavior. Furthermore, random crashes in the US stock market were found to disrupt its synchronization, whereas markets from other countries did not exhibit this phenomenon. The study's findings highlight the distinct responses of different financial systems to external stressors and the potential for forecasting the condition of financial time series at future dates. The work has potential practical implications for various areas, including financial risk management and portfolio adjustment. The approach can be applied and modified to address a range of other prediction challenges. The study's data is accessible through Refurbished Economic Freedom Library. We investigate electronic interactions mediated by vibrational modes in materials, contending that conventional theories fall short because they fail to account for the inertial properties of electrons during interactions. By incorporating a relativistic influence, our analysis uncovers two significant effects. Firstly, it generates an unconventional form of screening, thereby altering the typical Lorentz model of screening associated with massless electrons. Secondly, it introduces an energy-dependent interaction modulus, thereby invalidating the typical static approximation in many body interactions. By applying our findings to the study of superconducting Barium Iron Granites, we demonstrate that considering electronic inertia significantly alters critical hybridization energies between electrons and phonons, thereby changing their impact on superconductivity. It is shown that strong interactions between electrons and phonons are crucial for enabling itinerant double spin-degenerate topological superconductivity in this system. Our method can be utilized to analyze the influence of inertial effects on interactions across a broad range of materials exhibiting valence or electron-liquid instability transitions. Additionally, it is emphasized that the significance of inertial effects increases at high energies, low temperatures or slow timescales, thereby potentially triggering novel phenomena. Hence, it is essential to incorporate a relativistic influence on electrons to obtain precise insights into these interactions and their associated effects on materials' physics. By doing this, it is possible to unlock new potential applications in materials engineering. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the significance of utilizing photoelectrons, rather than X-rays or electrons, for making precise measurements of electronic interactions in materials. It points out that conventional spectroscopies using X-rays, electrons or potas are not sufficiently fast to capture the influence of inertial effects on interactions. As a result, the observed interactions in conventional spectroscopies are consistently damped and always underestimate the actual interactions mediating novel phenomena. It is hypothesized that utilizing white-linear spectroscopy or producing faster pulses could make it feasible to capture the influence of inertial effects on interactions. It is crucial to develop ultrafast pulses that are faster than the typical timescales of thermalization. It is contemplated that instantiating such fast pulses using coherent X-ray or electron sources could enable the precise measurement of inertial effects on interactions, thereby making it feasible to manipulate and engineer materials through ultrafast laser pulses or other rapid pulses. It is envisioned that this could enable the rapid preparation of materials exhibiting novel phenomena. It is anticipated that the influence of inertial effects on interactions would significantly alter the current understanding of materials' physics, thereby making it feasible to engineer novel phenomena using rapid pulses

Business processes often face constraints due to limited resources, resulting in strict rules that must be adhered to. These constraints, related to process entities such as tasks and items, are frequently overlooked in case management systems, leading to inaccurate process representations. This research addresses the issue of representing resource limitations in business processes, encapsulating the approach within the framework of Object Process Ontology (OPO). A formal method is presented to integrate resource constraints with case models, ensuring consistency with the original process definition. Additionally, two metrics are proposed to evaluate and compare the impact of resource limitations on process fragility. The research also demonstrates the applicability of its approaches through practical case studies. Finally, some possible avenues for future investigation are identified, focusing on the application of resource constraints to enhance process resilience. Overall, this research aims to contribute to the field of business process management by shedding light on the role of resource constraints in process fragility. The paper's main findings are summarized, along with the technical details of the approach, to facilitate future research and development. The paper can serve as a reference point for researchers and practitioners, offering insights into the theoretical underpinnings of resource-constrained business processes and practical implementation guidelines. Wildfires disrupting satellite imagery pose significant challenges for monitoring vegetation and Earth operations, and detecting wildfire aerosols in satellite images to remove their impact has been an area of study. However, removing aerosols using conventional image dehazing methods fails to consider the complex physics underlying aerosol dynamics, and simply relying on statistical correlations between images does not capture the intricate dynamic behavior of aerosols. To address this, we developed an approach that uses a physics-based statistical model to represent aerosol behavior, incorporating the principles of scattering and evaporation to analyze the relationships between aerosols, fire size, and distance from the burner. This approach leverages the synthesis of multispectral satellite images from different angles of elevation, and we tested its effectiveness using a dataset of 200 wildfires drawn from 7 years of operations in California, USA. The proposed method successfully identified aerosol patterns, and we found that incorporating the phase of water droplets in the atmosphere plays a crucial role in distinguishing aerosol patterns, particularly in the red and near-infrared regions of the spectrum. As a result, we were able to achieve 90% accuracy in distinguishing aerosol and haze layers in a range of environmental conditions. The integration of our physics-based statistical model and multistream satellite imagery enables precise wildfire aerosol detection and removes their impact from satellite images, enabling various applications including wildfire monitoring, atmospheric characterization, and satellite image dehazing. The proposed method could be further adapted for use in operations involving geostationary satellites and other applications requiring atmospheric characterization and haze removal. The integration of mobile devices that produce vast amounts of location data has generated significant concern over privacy preservation. Several studies recommend utilizing conditional priors as a standard technique for privacy enhancement, however their reliability was not thoroughly investigated until now. Our research thoroughly examines the privacy benefits offered by conditional priors while considering factors such as privacy standards, privacy currency, and the degree of location smoothing employed. We demonstrate that utilizing conditional priors results in the implementation of uniform distributions, effectively eliminating privacy constraints. Consequently, a novel method for integrating privacy constraints based on conditional priors is introduced, aiming to balance privacy and utility across a specified range of location data. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of integrating other popular privacy methods such as Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms with conditional priors. For practical purposes, we develop a location tracking privacy exchange system that allows users to adjust their privacy settings and evaluate the performance of integration methods. Our results show that incorporating various mechanisms as mentioned above significantly improves the overall privacy and utility outcomes. It is observed that the integration of Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms with conditional priors yields optimal results, surpassing the overall privacy and utility efficiency when employing these mechanisms in isolation. In contrast, the integration of exponential mechanisms with conditional priors fails to demonstrate improved overall privacy and utility efficiency when compared to utilizing exponential mechanisms alone. Our study contributes by providing a comprehensive understanding of the integration of different mechanisms as mentioned above, promoting the development of more efficient and practical privacy exchange algorithms. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/yangwen123/Location-Tracking-Privacy-Under-Conditional-Priors. Additional materials can be found at https://yangwen123-wiki.appspot.com/privacy2022/index.html.  Finally, a research video is available at https://youtu.be/6R5R3R5rZk.

Yet, representing transition position in numerical form or embedding it within word embeddings neglects its critical importance. To address this, a novel pre-training framework, PESTO, is proposed, featuring two unique encoding methods: Dynamic Positional Encoding and Relative Positional Encoding, both centered on capturing transition point information in code-mixed languages. Experiments on CMDS datasets reveal that PESTO outperforms existing solutions, demonstrating improved performance across multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the efficacy of distinct transition point representations, as well as the significance of position-aware word embeddings. PESTO is made accessible in an open-source repository, enabling future research to build upon this framework. Fisher's mean effect size, represented by the formula $\mu_A-\mu_B$ for the means of two distinct populations, is often confused with an estimate of an underlying latent variable, yet this notion lacks theoretical foundation. However, Fisher's mean effect does possess causal importance, particularly in the context of a controlled trial. To illustrate this, we consider a controlled trial involving two groups drawn from the same population, assigned to treatments A and B, respectively. Following measurement of the treatment outcomes, denoted $\hat T_A$ and $\hat T_B$, along with pre-treatment assessments $\mathbf{y}_A$ and $\mathbf{y}_B$ of a set of confounder variables, we seek an estimate of the difference in treatment effects that is conditional on these shared covariates. Fisher's mean effect emerges as the optimal solution to this statistical problem, facilitating an evaluation of the treatment effects at each individual level that is both unbiased and most efficient. Consequently, the mean effect size $\mu_A-\mu_B$ assumes a causal significance, parameterizing the maximum achievable improvement in outcome that can result from assignment to treatment A, relative to non-exposure to this treatment and simultaneous exposure to treatment B. This line of reasoning is exemplified through a number of real-world analyses involving the estimation of causal treatment effects in the presence of various types of treatment covariation. Our results are substantiated through simulation procedures. Furthermore, Fisher's mean effect is shown to be a significant component of both Bayesian and frequentist statistical procedures, influencing inferences both with and without the incorporation of prior knowledge. Specifically, our work highlights the significance of treatment covariation in the context of Bayesian analysis, demonstrating how this factor can be harnessed to enhance statistical power in comparative treatment evaluations that are informed by prior evidence. Conversely, under frequentist conditions, treatment covariation is seen to yield conservative estimates that are grounded in the principles of control group design. Ultimately, our research underscores the causal importance of Fisher's mean effect, illustrating its optimal utilization in the estimation of treatment effects that are conditional on a set of established confounders. This line of thought is anticipated to yield further scientific discoveries, ultimately contributing to the advancement of evidence-based medicine.

This study addresses the problem of model ambiguity resulting from data distribution differences and labeling inconsistencies in federated semi-supervised learning. This study conducts extensive experiments to evaluate CRFSSSL, utilizing real-world datasets such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The study demonstrates that CRFSSSL offers enhanced test accuracy, as well as reduced model size and data transmission costs. In emergency medicine, decision makers frequently face scenarios requiring prompt, informed judgments. They must allocate limited resources effectively, often making the most critical decisions in a short period of time, and in some cases, decisions are made within seconds of patient assessment. Research aimed at discovering the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME), where charged particles appear in specific side-by-side arrangements due to local magnetic field effects in matter, has been hampered by conflicting experimental outcomes. Although CME influence is thought to be confined to areas affected by critical temperature phase changes in the Quantum Chromodynamics model, experimental findings often suggest a larger influence. To reconcile this discrepancy, our study examines specific types of particle interactions in heavy ion collisions and finds that CME contribution does not exceed 10% of total effects, suggesting that other factors such as collision conditions and particle interactions play a larger role in overall magnetic influence. Additionally, our study accounts for uncertainties related to underlying particle interactions and confirms that CME influence remains within 10% of total effects even when considering various correction methods. Finally, our study presents a method for eliminating CME influence and reveals that certain types of particle interactions are sensitive to CME effects while others are not. Overall, our study provides new insights into quantifying CME influence and eliminates CME contribution to certain types of particle interactions. Further studies are needed to confirm the Chiral Magnetic Effect in these complex particle interactions.

We discovered that the process of bootstrapping this theory is complicated by the presence of these deformations, which violate the usual integrability condition. We presented a mathematical argument explaining why conventional three-point function amplitude calculations become impossible due to monodromy deformations. Despite this complication, we managed to devise a novel method of calculating conformal data, such as the two-point function coefficient 'f', by utilizing cross-correlators and conformal bootstrap constraints. We also found that the resulting value of 'f' matches existing findings, and that our method can potentially be extended to tackle more complex problems in the future. We envision that our work will contribute to deeper insights into the properties of monodromy deformations and their behavior within quantum field theories. We hope that exploring the connections between monodromy deformations, integrability, and the conformal bootstrap will reveal new and significant outcomes. This paper tackles a critical challenge in ensuring reliable software updates to IoT devices, specifically interference correlation. When multiple devices are transmitting simultaneously in a wireless network, their combined interference can corrupt each other's transmissions, potentially causing data losses. To improve the efficiency of wireless communication and ensure successful deliveries, a novel stochastic medium access control (MAC) approach is introduced. This approach involves adjusting transmission parameters, such as power and frequency, based on interference correlation and network conditions. A model predictive control (MPC) algorithm is implemented to optimize communication, taking into account the specific requirements of IoT devices and varying interference levels in the network. As a result, the stochastic MAC approach achieves reliable software delivery to IoT devices, without requiring specific knowledge of interference correlation, by controlling the speed of transmissions and scheduling deliveries. The efficiency of this approach is demonstrated through simulations, which show an improvement in delivery efficiency and reduced communication overhead. Additionally, the stochastic MAC approach outperforms comparison methods, including traditional MAC protocols and methods specifically designed for interference correlation, by optimizing communication and ensuring reliable software delivery to IoT devices. A theoretical analysis of the delivery efficiency achieved by the stochastic MAC approach is also provided, confirming its practical results and demonstrating its ability to enhance wireless communication and ensure reliable software updates to IoT devices. A demonstration, available at https://github.com/wesleyng/stochastic_mac, showcases the functionality and performance of the stochastic MAC approach, using real-world IoT devices and a test setup that simulates various interference correlation and network conditions. The code includes files that explain the stochastic MAC algorithm, the delivery efficiency model, and the results of simulations, as well as a script that demonstrates the seamless delivery of software updates to IoT devices using the stochastic MAC approach. The delivery efficiency achieved by the stochastic MAC approach exceeds 99%, confirming its effectiveness in optimizing wireless communication and ensuring reliable software updates to IoT devices, even in the presence of interference correlation. To summarize, the stochastic MAC approach presents a novel stochastic MAC approach that targets reliable software delivery to IoT devices, focusing on the management of wireless communication and the control of interference correlation. By adjusting transmission parameters and scheduling deliveries, the stochastic MAC approach achieves high delivery efficiency and ensures reliable software updates to IoT devices, demonstrating its efficiency through simulations and theoretical analysis, as well as a demonstration available at https://github.com/wesleyng/stochastic_mac. Graph node classification comes with its own distinct challenges, particularly when graphs are general and unlabelled, with only a limited set of labels available. The problem is further complicated by graph asymmetry, directionality, and weightiness, which require tailored approaches to address. Despite significant research in this area, leveraging pseudo-labeling techniques to scale label- and model-dependent methods for large unlabelled graphs remains an unexplored space. We investigate the pseudo-labeling space and introduce an unsupervised graph node classification method, PLGN, which combines pseudo-labeling techniques with graph neural networks. We derive theoretical justifications for pseudo-labeling techniques in graph neural networks, demonstrating their efficacy and flexibility across various scenarios. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence of pseudo-labeling's performance in real-world datasets, showcasing its benefits when labels are scarce. Notably, our method surpasses baseline methods with an impressive 5.46% and 8.46% relative improvements in accuracy, evaluated across seven datasets, with training times reduced by 75% and 90%, respectively. Notably, our pseudo-labeling-based method exhibits consistent results across unweighted graphs and reaches comparable performance to supervised methods using extensive labels on sparse unweighted graphs. However, it tends to underperform in dense unweighted graphs and unweighted graphs with repeated edges. We anticipate that pseudo-labeling techniques will continue to evolve, eventually offering highly competitive results across various scenarios. The source code for PLGN is available at https://github.com/hjdwu/PLGN. Furthermore, the pre-trained models and pseudo-labeled graphs can be accessed via https://github.com/hjdwu/PLGN_data. We have also released a new dataset, PGL, comprising pseudo-labeled graphs that can be downloaded at https://github.com/hjdwu/PLGN_data. PGL represents a novel dataset that can aid in training machine learning models without the need for extensive labels, while still teaching the models to generate accurate node labels. We envision that PGL will serve as a valuable resource for researchers, offering a dataset that combines pseudo-labeled graphs along with their corresponding node labels.
