One key factor contributing to the success of recommender systems is effectively addressing users' diverse information needs and preferences. To this end, research in recommender systems has focused on incorporating various approaches that leverage user-provided content and past behavior to generate personalized recommendations. Despite their merits, existing systems have inherent limitations, including reliance on incomplete or inaccurate content information and the inability to capture inherent relationships among items. Furthermore, existing systems fail to attend to users' evolving preferences and provide personalized recommendations in a dynamic and ever-changing environment. To address these shortcomings, this research presents a novel hybrid approach called Hybrid-Context-Aware, which integrates a content-based method that extracts meaningful item characteristics from user-supplied content and a collaborative filtering method that generates recommendations based on the collective wisdom of the community. We implement a comprehensive evaluation strategy, comprising a systematic assessment of content-based recommendations, a meta-learning approach, and a dynamic community-wisdom model, to refine and validate our architecture. The results of extensive experimentation with real-world data demonstrate the Hybrid-Context-Aware architecture's ability to outperform state-of-the-art systems in terms of precision, effectiveness, and efficiency. The incorporation of dynamic user profiles, content-based information, and a contextual awareness model yields significantly higher accuracy and more relevant recommendations. Moreover, the Hybrid-Context-Aware architecture exhibits a more linear and consistent improvement in recommendation quality over time. The community-wisdom model's ability to capture item characteristics from user-supplied content and the integration of contextual awareness and content-based information in the Hybrid-Context-Aware architecture are key factors contributing to the development of higher-quality and more relevant recommendations. Ultimately, the Hybrid-Context-Aware architecture can serve as a versatile and efficient platform for designing dynamic and content-aware recommender systems that prioritize effectiveness and efficiency. The integration of contextual awareness and content-based information can lead to higher-quality and more relevant recommendations and a more consistent and linear improvement in recommendation quality over time. The Hybrid-Context-Aware architecture can be employed to enhance existing recommender systems and provide more accurate and personalized recommendations in a dynamic environment. The models and evaluation methods presented in this research can be utilized to refine and enhance the performance of recommender systems in various contexts. The integration of meta-learning and Hybrid-Context-Aware approaches offers promising possibilities for enhancing the effectiveness and efficiency of recommender systems. To further explore these possibilities, we plan to conduct further experimentation, including the development of dynamic user profiles through social network analysis and the incorporation of additional contextual awareness models and content-based information methods. A key concept in characterising the temporal behaviour of systems is the 'observing interval'. This concept was initially introduced to define different types of system states, based on how frequently certain conditions are met within a specific time frame. Building on previous work, this study expands upon existing research by refining the definition of observing intervals and exploring several related properties. Notably, the new research establishes a logical connection between observing intervals and notable system transition points, as well as demonstrates the computability of intervals under specific criteria. A key contribution of this study is the introduction of a new class of systems, 'polytope systems', as a primary object of analysis. Polytope systems are systems whose state evolution over time is constrained by a set of linearly-related variables, as their values constantly change. These systems can model a variety of real-world systems, as their state variables are often related through linear combinations. Various properties of observing intervals in polytope systems were investigated, as well as their relationship with classical 'ultimately periodically' properties. A key challenge associated with verifying these properties in systems with complex nonlinear relationships between state variables remains unresolved and serves as a focal point for potential future research. Moreover, the study presents a suite of algorithms designed to determine whether a system satisfies specific temporal characteristics. As a means of validating the introduced concepts and evaluating their practical utility, several practical examples were drawn from a range of domains, including discrete-time systems, systems described by Boolean equations, and systems whose evolution over time is constrained by linear relationships between their state variables. Finally, the new research examines key distinctions between various system time-characteristics and establishes a logical connection between these properties and system readability. A particular class of systems, 'ultimately periodically' systems, as well as its extension to model systems whose underlying dynamics are affected by random variables, were also examined. This paper explores how polynomial equations can be solved using linear equations, under conditions of uncertainty. More specifically, we consider the scenario where coefficients in linear equations are randomly incorrect. Given a polynomial equation of degree d, we establish a lower bound on the number of linear equations required for verification, equal to d^2 + dd. This lower bound surpasses previous estimates, including Zamaere et al.'s result (around dd^2) and recent findings by Guruswami et al. (around d + log(d)^d). Additionally, we introduce an 'early stopping' technique, allowing for efficient verification by identifying distinct roots. This involves linear equation solving, followed by verification among potential roots. Under certain conditions, this process requires significantly fewer linear equations than total root count. This technique surpasses previous efficiency estimates, including Dizhe et al.'s result (around d log(d) linear equations), and recent improvements by Guruswami et al. (around d + log(d)^2 linear equations). This research combines the early stopping technique with our lower bound, yielding a new efficient method for polynomial equation solving, using approximately dd linear equations. Numerical relativity researchers face significant challenges when initializing their simulations due to limited data availability. This leads them to make inaccurate assumptions - a major limitation of current numerical relativity approaches. In principle, allowing initial conditions to evolve freely should ultimately enable the desired target state, yet the rapid early stage of simulations typically renders these methods ineffective. In this work, we propose introducing variations in initial conditions using a novel technique called Changing the Toes, which stands for altering the initial spatial arrangement of matter in relativistic gravitational wave source simulations. These variations result in meaningful changes to the resulting gravitational wave spectra, allowing us to identify suitable combinations that efficiently produce target-based waves with specified characteristics. This technique has numerous applications and benefits, including potentially decreasing simulation duration, minimizing necessary grid sizes, and thereby achieving significant cost savings. We successfully demonstrated its potential by developing and presenting a method to produce numerical relativity simulations with prescribed gravitational wave amplitude and frequency. This approach might also be used in the future to produce ensembles of initial conditions that can subsequently be combined using machine learning techniques to produce specific target-based waves. In summary, Changing the Toes offers a groundbreaking method of initializing simulations that enables numerical relativity researchers to efficiently produce waves with desired features, thereby opening up new avenues for numerical relativity research. We provide code modifications to support this technique in the GitHub repository: https://github.com/CTTK/CTTK/tree/main and share the details of the used dataset in "numerical_reality_dataset.hdf5" at the same location. For a specific inner product space equipped with a continuous basis, we demonstrate that a sparse solution can be uniquely reconstructed from its moments with respect to any arbitrary continuous set that covers its support. Furthermore, our method is adaptable and can be implemented using conventional iterative techniques similar to L1-minimization algorithms. Additionally, we show that enforcing a Lipschitz-continuity constraint on the basis results in representability by a finite basis set, thus providing an alternative approach to existing results. Finally, we discuss how our findings generalize the concept of null-controllability in control theory. However, we also identify a critical limitation - the existence of non-unique representations for differently equipped subspaces of infinite dimension. To address this limitation, we develop a novel "average support" concept that selects a single representative for each collection of mutually exclusive sparse solutions. Consequently, we derive an operator that outputs the unique support for any given inner product with a continuous basis. Our work covers a broad range of applications, and we subsequently apply it to the control of ordinary differential equations and partial differential equations. Lastly, we suggest that our methods and results can be extended to other sparsity-promoting optimization problems. To train the complex Deep Neural Networks that power Image Classification, researchers turn to model-parallel training, a technique that distributes the computation across multiple GPUs. However, current model-parallel training methods typically rely on expert knowledge and tailored modifications to the learning process, limiting their practical application. In response, we introduce Regional Reviewer Training, a novel approach that automates the model-parallel training of Deep Neural Networks using complex learning schedules. Our innovative method relies on a simple yet effective technique: periodically summarizing the intermediate computation with a summary tensor, and using this tensor to inform subsequent training steps. Our approach is inspired by the concepts of virtual place and reviewer, and can be applied to a wide range of models and image datasets. In our experiments, Regional Reviewer Training outperforms traditional model-parallel training methods, and competes favorably with decentralized approaches, achieving a significant improvement of 15% and 12% in top-1 accuracy for ResNet50 and MobileNet on the ImageNet dataset, and reducing computation costs by 67% and 58% for batch sizes of 32 and 256. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/huijaing/Regional_Reviewer_Training. In addition, we establish Model Parallel, a comprehensive evaluation benchmark of deep neural networks that can be found at https://mplauncher.github.io/. This benchmark includes 40 different models and 7 image datasets, and uses a unified interface to present the results of various training protocols. Our approach, Regional Reviewer Training, is also integrated into the MP-Laucher framework, allowing researchers to easily compare the performance of different training protocols on the datasets and models of their choice. In a word, Regional Reviewer Training is a novel approach that automates the model-parallel training of deep neural networks, and outperforms traditional model-parallel training methods, competing favorably with decentralized approaches, and is now publicly available as part of the MP-Laucher framework at https://mp-laucher.github.io/. In particular, researchers can find the details of our approach and the benchmark in the papers "Automating Deep Neural Network Training with Computational Steganography" (NeurIPS 2020) and "Model Parallel (MP-Laucher): A Unified Framework for Training Deep Neural Networks on Multiple GPUs" (ArXiv 2020). Transport infrastructure administrators face a critical challenge of determining which energy network links require upgrades to meet future demands. This critical decision necessitates accurate predictions of network usage and performance. Currently, there is no universally reliable forecasting method, leading many estimates are based on past trends, which can be unreliable in the face of changing conditions. In this paper, we present a novel approach based on quantum physics, called the Quantum Energy Network, which can predict energy demand with high precision and reduce the cost of upgrades by identifying the most necessary links. We put this method to the test using realistic scenarios modeled on actual energy networks. The results show that the Quantum Energy Network can predict energy usage with less error than traditional methods and pinpoint the most crucial links requiring upgrades. We also investigate how varying the quantum parameters affects prediction accuracy. The findings confirm that the Quantum Energy Network is a viable and efficient tool for making data-driven decisions in energy network management. This breakthrough approach can be adapted to various administrative tasks involving forecasting, expanding the scope of quantum applications beyond computational problems. With further development, the Quantum Energy Network has the potential to revolutionize the administration of transport infrastructure and numerous other decision-making processes. The search for fundamental physical laws may become obsolete if physics can be derived from experimental data, as suggested by the data-driven approach. This theory claims that all physical laws are inherent in the data and can be uncovered through analysis. By examining data sets of different sizes, the theory's hypotheses about universal properties were tested, but inconsistencies were found, revealing that the data-driven approach is unviable. This critique is based on two areas: first, the preconceived idea of selecting suitable and limited data sets; and second, the reliance on inductive reasoning, which is inherently flawed. Two types of reasoning that could lead to a deeper understanding of physical laws are discussed as alternatives: one that uses data to eliminate incorrect hypotheses, and another that applies statistical methods to identify patterns and correlations. Ultimately, a distinct research strategy is required to explore this new paradigm. If successful, this endeavor may ultimately lead to a unified theory, but the pursuit should be approached with caution and skepticism. A statistical examination of the Nobel Prize awards in Physics is also conducted, revealing that the selection of research areas is not random, and Nobel laureates are more likely to receive further recognition. This analysis demonstrates that inducing general laws from specific data has limited value, and exploratory, skeptical investigation is necessary to uncover new insights in physics. Two specific examples illustrate the power of skeptical investigation: the Anderson-Darling test and the Bessels inequality. This critique is supplemented by an open-source mathematical software package that can be used to repeat the analysis, enabling further collaboration and reflection. Additionally, this study examines how the paradigm of inducing general laws from specific data has shaped the research agenda in physics, and it proposes an alternative methodology based on the Anderson-Darling test. This critical examination is accompanied by an open-source mathematical software package that can be used to replicate the analysis, facilitating collaboration and reflection. It is observed that inducing general laws can lead to biased research goals, and two case studies are presented to demonstrate how skeptical investigation can yield new insights. Ultimately, the authors argue that diversity analysis offers a novel and valuable perspective on optimization equilibria. In large groups of people, creating suitable living arrangements can be a complex task. To address this challenge, we develop a mathematical framework for allocating space among members of a trio under specific preference patterns. Our approach relies on the concept of additive divisibility in preferences, allowing us to determine whether a set of individually reasonable arrangements can collectively be realized and whether larger groups can be accommodated with these same preference patterns. Our results indicate that this possibility exists for groups of three and four, but it is unlikely in larger groups. To verify the efficacy of our model, we employed a simple and efficient algorithm to find arrangements for the Steady Roommates problem. Our approach combines techniques from linear programming and graph theory to solve this problem in a practical scenario. Our findings indicate that this model provides a practical and efficient solution to the steady roommate problem. Furthermore, we explored the extension of our model to larger social networks. Our analysis indicates that arranging meetings in a sequential order can improve the overall satisfaction of the arrangement, and that a particular structure in the preference graph is crucial for solving the steady roommate problem. Ultimately, our model discloses a significant connection between the concept of additive divisibility in preferences and the arrangement of meetings. To illustrate our findings, we examined a real-life example involving a small social group. Our analysis shows that our model can identify a suitable arrangement that maximizes the overall satisfaction. Our work contributes to the body of literature on preference-based models, providing a new theoretical framework that can efficiently tackle the steady roommate problem under specific preference patterns and extending existing models in practical scenarios. Additionally, our results are likely generalizable to other arrangement problems, and our model provides a practical and efficient solution to these challenges. The PHENIX collaboration has investigated photon-hadron correlations in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at a collision energy of 200 GeV. These correlations were examined for direct photons, and the results indicate that the associated hadrons show a faster yield in Au$+$Au compared to $d$$+$Au collisions, particularly at higher hadron transverse momentum levels. This yield excess is attributed to jet-medium interactions as they cross through the hot and cold media respectively. Furthermore, the observed increase in hadron $p_T$ can be attributed to the jet that is paired with the direct photon, while the lower $p_T$ hadrons are likely a result of the jet interacting with the Au$+$Au collision medium. Additionally, the hadron $x_T$ distribution shifts towards higher values of $x_T$ in Au$+$Au, which is consistent with the idea of jets being glazed or thermalized as they emerge from the medium, resulting in the transfer of some of the jet's energy to the collision medium. This phenomenon is observed across all centralities except the 5-10\% range, which suggests that the jet energy loss is not dependent on the location of the jet within the Au$+$Au collision system. Even with advanced adaptive optics systems, the performance of ground-based telescopes can still be limited by the inherent distortions caused by the atmosphere. Although AO systems can effectively address certain types of speckles born from detector noise, others stemming from uncorrected aberrations pose a challenge. This paper presents the first experimental results of an AO technique known as Rapid Atmospheric Self-coherent AO, which aims to address these residual speckles. This technique utilizes the inherent spatial coherence of speckles to track and correct even the most persistent aberrations. In our testbed experiments using a 50-inch diagonal testbed, we successfully demonstrated the implementation of RASC-AO and achieved impressive results, specifically focusing on mitigating the high-velocity speckles that AO systems often struggle with. With RASC-AO, we achieved a substantial reduction of more than 3 times in the standard deviation of speckle-related performance loss, resulting in speckle-related performance loss quantified by the alpha AO parameter of as low as 0.0006. This successful demonstration of RASC-AO paves the way for its utilization in various applications, including astronomy and other fields. This technique could potentially provide a means to eliminate AO and enable the direct application of Coherent AO and other high-performance AO techniques. Additionally, this project holds potential for collaborations with industry in areas such as defense and medicine. In particular, RASC-AO may facilitate the development of high-performance, wide-field-of-view imaging systems that could potentially capture images of objects thousands of kilometers apart. This technology could also enable the creation of advanced, high-resolution imaging systems for aerial and ground use. In the context of astronomy, RASC-AO could allow for larger telescopes, including those with collectivities of multiple 8-meter diameter mirrors, to achieve higher resolution and collect more light than currently possible under atmospheric restrictions. This could result in numerous breakthroughs, including the detection of distant planets and alien life, and the observation of the birth and death of nearby and distant stars. More information on the RASC-AO project can be found at rasc-ao.org. In the near future, we intend to enhance our testbed by increasing its field-of-view and incorporating a 200-inch diagonal, thereby significantly expanding its potential for a wide array of applications. This will include the direct capture of images using RASC-AO at new, higher spatial resolutions. Our testbed will provide a means for demonstrating the effectiveness of RASC-AO under varying conditions to astronomers and other scientists.

When conducting a meta-analysis with paired data points from the same study, researchers face challenges associated with non-diagonal covariance matrices. To overcome these difficulties, researchers often employ approximate methods such as ordinary mixed-effects (OME) and ordinary partner mean-variation (OPM) estimators. Although these approximations simplify the analysis but introduce bias, we present a new family of estimators, called cluster-sturdy estimators, which leverage the available study-level data to counteract this bias. Specifically, we derive expressions for the bias and develop a method to eliminate it, resulting in more efficient estimates. We compare the proposed estimators to existing alternatives through simulation studies and demonstrate their utility in a real-world application involving paired data from 24 studies. Furthermore, we extend the existing theory to accommodate diverse model specifications, including heterogeneous data, unbalanced sample sizes, and uncorrelated residual variances. To facilitate practical implementation, we develop a publicly available R package providing the necessary functionality. Ultimately, the proposed estimators offer a valuable improvement over existing methods in providing more accurate effect size estimates, improved confidence intervals, and correct type-I error rates. Key words: Cluster-sturdy, Bond, and Reikvam estimators, bias correction, efficient estimation, meta-analysis, paired data, heterogeneity, unbalanced data, correlated residual variances. Current simulation methods for particle collisions either use a single time step or fixed collision durations. However, employing a fixed collision duration may lead to inaccurate particle positions, while using a single time step limits simulation throughput. To address these issues, this work introduces a new integration method, influencing particle positions based on the relative velocity of colliding particles. Consequently, this method enables simulations to utilize larger time steps that align with physical collision periods, thereby boosting efficiency and producing more precise results. Additionally, this method retains the accuracy of single time-step methods and avoids the limitations associated with using fixed collision durations. To validate this new method, simulations involving colliding particles of various types were conducted. These experiments demonstrated the advantages of the new method in terms of efficiency and outcome accuracy. Specifically, the new method produced results identical to those obtained with single time-step methods but achieved a nearly 50% increase in efficiency when simulating the collision of two identical polymer particles. Furthermore, this method yielded more precise results for the post-collision positions of particles undergoing plastic deformation, thereby supplementing existing simulation techniques. Although this method incurs a greater computational cost compared to fixed collision-duration methods, it demonstrates the potential to greatly enhance outcome accuracy, making it a valuable tool for simulations involving particle collisions. To facilitate the adoption of this new method, all relevant simulation code has been openly accessible, allowing researchers to perform replicate studies. A potential drawback of this method is its heightened sensitivity to integration errors, particularly when handling soft-body collisions where the deformation of particles may lead to temporary overlaps exceeding the specified tolerance. However, this can be mitigated through the implementation of either kinetic or conservative penetration reduction. By integrating either of these techniques, the method presented here can efficiently handle the complex mechanics of particle collisions with enhanced precision and minimal computational overhead. Kinetic penetration reduction, a more straightforward yet computationally inexpensive option, was found to sufficiently eliminate integration errors and produce very accurate results. Conversely, conservative penetration reduction, although computationally more demanding, was determined to be essential for accurately capturing the detailed mechanical interactions inherent to particle collisions. A key observation made during the course of these studies is that both penetration reduction techniques can significantly boost the efficiency and accuracy of the method, essentially eliminating integration errors and producing results indistinguishable from single time-step methods. Parallal processing supercomputers rely heavily on fault-tolerant storage systems that can withstood multiple disk failures. For this, RAID6 has been widely used but has drawbacks such as performance loss and data obstruction after just two failures, requiring a switch to higher RAID levels with increased storage usage and costs. Our research introduces Crash Fault Tolerant file systems that allow algorithmic decision-making and temporary performance compromises after disk crashes to ensure data accessibility until failing disks are replaced. Our approach combines static and dynamic redundancy algorithms to enable continued file system operation with reduced performance during disk recovery, rather than total data loss. CTFS utilizes multiple algorithms such as Parity Spread, Multi-Dimensional Modulo, and Erasure Coding to ensure data reliability. Experiments using workloads from the HPC Application Working Group reveal minimal effects on file system performance, with some increases in metadata overhead. CTFS achieves successful file system operation despite crashes and efficient data retrieval, with results below linear trend for performance. Moreover, CTFS incurs only 0.62% additional metadata overhead. Ongoing research focuses on integrating new algorithms to further enhance Crash Fault Tolerant file system reliability, performance, and efficiency. Moreover, software modifications to existing file systems are being made to enable CTFS, with analyses and assessments of CTFS based on data availability. Future developments aim to integrate CTFS into the Linux kernel for widespread integration and use. Lastly, research is underway to quantify the extent of performance degradation, including numerical evaluations of CTFS algorithmic options and evaluations of alternative algorithms. This research lays the foundation for a robust and efficient Crash Fault Tolerant file system. Several key challenges need to be addressed: (a) algorithmic temporary performance compromises may lead to data obstruction; (b) software integration may require significant modifications to the file system code; (c) evaluating algorithmic options during runtime may delay decision-making; (d) algorithmic temporary performance compromises may undermine the reliability of fault-tolerant storage. We propose CTFS-R, an algorithmic strategy that addresses these challenges by prioritizing data reliability over performance during runtime. CTFS-R utilizes runtime information to quickly identify files that need temporary performance compromises and rely on algorithmic temporary performance compromises only when absolutely necessary. Moreover, CTFS-R uses a reliability-aware strategy that prioritizes algorithmic temporary performance compromises over metadata overhead. The category's morphisms are shown to be equivalent to the continuous functions between these spaces that satisfy certain continuity conditions. Selecting the appropriate test cases for verification is a crucial and complex process in software development, particularly for systems comprising a large number of functions. Typically, this process relies on analytical models or simulation outcomes to identify which test cases to run. However, this can result in extremely large sets of required test cases. To tackle this issue, we propose an innovative approach that uses parallel processing of test cases based on unique value decomposition. This technique enables the efficient execution of a large number of parallel procedures, allowing each one to handle a distinct set of test cases. As a result, the overall computational time is significantly reduced, making it simpler to select and execute the necessary test cases for software development. This proposed method has been successfully applied and evaluated in the ParTest framework for practical purposes. Documents and source code related to this article are publicly available at the specified URLs. Evaluation results indicate that the proposed method significantly decreases the overall computational time for ParTest case selection. This is achieved by leveraging the capabilities of multiple CPU cores, leading to a linear relationship between the number of available cores and the computational efficiency. This proposal's innovative contribution lies in the parallel processing of test cases, effectively utilizing the capabilities of modern computers through unique value decomposition. Suicidal ideation is a serious mental health issue that requires intense surveillance due to a high recurrence rate and potentially fatal consequences. Effective detection through machine learning could significantly lower mortality rates by identifying high-risk individuals. Previous studies have utilized single-data-source approaches, but combining multiple data streams has the potential to significantly increase detection accuracy. This research presents a novel deep learning framework that integrates information from electroencephalogram, functional magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical history to predict suicidal thoughts. This unique combination is analyzed in a combined dataset from two sources, the Affective Computing Challenge and the AVM database, totaling 1,rockiness datasets with 348 instances. This study introduces three novel deep sequential models: the SUICIDE-BGRU, SUICIDE-BGRU_EEG, and SUICIDE-BGRU_Clinical models. Experimental results indicate that integrating multiple data streams surpasses individual data types in predictive accuracy, with a notable 6.66% improvement in overall accuracy from the baseline EEG model. The proposed deep sequential model demonstrates promising results, achieving 57.89% overall accuracy when trained on combined data, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, quantitative evaluations using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve reveal high success rates among top-performing models, reaching 86.32% accuracy with the SUICIDE-BGRU_Clinical model. This research presents novel deep sequential models that successfully integrate information from multiple data streams, yielding superior results and unlocking new possibilities for machine learning-based detection of suicidal thoughts. The proposed approach has potential applications in mental health surveillance, potentially lowering mortality rates. The study's datasets, models, and full code are publicly available at https://github.com/AhmedArab/FMRI-EEG-Clinical History Deep Sequential Model. This work utilizes a technique called skeletonization to extract detailed information about the structure of interfaces in complex fluid simulations. By applying a novel extension of a traditional skeletonization algorithm to volume datasets lacking a defined zero-isosurface, we're able to characterize the intricate geometry of interfaces in simulations involving multiple phases. This methodology enables the accurate quantification of interface properties such as branch points, junction points, and curvature. This method is utilized to analyze and quantify the effects of turbulence on droplet surfaces in a study of turbulent flow impinging on a plate. Results show increased deformation and a heightened number of pinch points on droplets due to turbulence. Furthermore, skeletons offer a compact representation of the droplet's geometry, allowing for the calculation of volumetric properties and offering a new framework for understanding the effects of turbulence on droplets. This work lays the foundation for the utilization of skeletonization in a variety of applications involving multiphase flows. With potential applications including the detection of pathogens based on their interaction with surfaces, understanding tumor cell spread, and enhancing heat transfer using droplets, this technique has far-reaching potential for modeling and simulating complex biological and engineering processes. We examine a peculiar class of disk galaxies experiencing significant warping, a subtype known as 'U' warsping. Our research expands upon prior studies by linking U type warping to three additional phenomena: jellyfish galaxies, tidal disruption, and spiral arm dissolution. By analyzing a randomly selected sample of 12,779 galaxies from the SDSS dataset, we discover that U type warping is more prevalent in larger clusters and has various morphological dependencies. It's also associated with higher star formation rates. Our findings suggest that U type warping, like tidal destruction and spiral arm dissolution, is linked to tidal forces, with the most severe cases resulting in spiral arm loss and star formation increases, ultimately leading to the transformation of U type galaxies into jellyfish galaxies. This analysis paves the way for a new theoretical framework in Section 5, where we propose that U type warping and tidal destruction are interconnected phenomena, akin to a continuum of the same process, and that jellyfish galaxies represent the most extreme outcome. This framework aims to offer a simplified, unified explanation at high-redshift. Additionally, we suggest that U type warping could be an early indicator of an impending tidal encounter, serving as a warning sign for the potential transformation of a galaxy into a jellyfish galaxy. By acknowledging this, we may be able to identify more jellyfish galaxies at the present time, ultimately allowing us to calculate the abundance of these galaxies throughout the universe's history. This research lays the groundwork for a forthcoming paper exploring a novel theoretical model designed to elucidate the proposed paradigm. To facilitate further exploration, we publicly share all our data and analysis at https://github.com/cco18/DeformedDiskGalaxies, including jupyter notebooks and a python script. Finally, we highlight that our research is likely confined to late-type galaxies due to the absence of early-type galaxies experiencing U type warping, and our findings may not be applicable to spiral galaxies with a higher disk-to-bulb ratio. In contrast, early-type galaxies are more susceptible to experiencing 'S' type warping. If a tidal force were the primary driver of U type warping, it is challenging to reconcile this phenomenon with the accepted understanding of early-type and late-type galaxies experiencing distinct types of warping. Conversely, late-type galaxies may be more resistant to tidal forces due to their lower central density. Rather than a tidal force, U type warping could be the result of a different mechanism, potentially linked to the formation of bars, and is likely accompanied by an increased likelihood of spiral arms

This mode is known as the silent frequency in group-15 element semiconductors. Calculations using density functional theory revealed that the chiral vibrational frequency is located above the fundamental gap. Additionally, the authors performed microscopic analyses on the chiral interaction and Bi-Bi bonding in the $A$Bi$_2$ crystals to provide a potential mechanism for observing the chiral vibrational mode via infrared absorption spectroscopy. This involves exciting the mode using linearly polarized light and detecting the resulting transmission changes. If successful, this could offer a pioneering approach to experimentally detecting silent modes in chiral systems. Based on the estimated values, the authors suggested that the chiral vibrational frequency could be observed in the RbBi$_2$ and CsBi$_2$ crystals, but not in the KBi$_2$ crystal due to its higher frequency. This study contributes to our understanding of chiral vibrational modes and silent modes in physics and chemistry. A key finding is that the two categories coincide when we exclude types that can be expressed as infinite sums (known as 'countable unions'). This result relies on a technical analysis involving the properties of minimal trees. A notable implication of this analysis is that it confirms the validity of a specific axiom type that had previously been speculated upon. In software and hardware design, natural language documentation is often used,
but its reliability is a concern due to the potential for inaccurate conclusions when
analyzing ambiguous design discussions. Typically, design dialogue conclusions are
evaluated based on their frequency, but this approach fails if the conclusions are
unreliable due to inconsistent information. To address this issue, we introduce a new
metric that assesses the robustness of design dialogue conclusions by calculating
the percentage of discussions that support these conclusions. This approach is
tested on applications from the Model Driven Architecture and hardware systems, by
comparing the robustness of the conclusions drawn from design dialogue analysis
and traditional frequency-based approaches. Results show that the new robustness
metric yields more accurate design dialogue analyses and enhances the reliability of
hardware system modeling. Moreover, this approach is adaptable to other domains
that employ natural language modeling. Experimental findings also reveal that more
natural language processing techniques need to be employed to further improve the
reliability of design dialogue conclusions in software and hardware design. Lastly, we
identify and separate implicit conclusions that emerge from design dialogue analysis
although not explicitly stated. We envision this work to contribute to establishing
a reliable foundation for natural language modeling in software and hardware design. 
This paper will be presented at ICSR 2022.

Research on analyzing the rate at which iterates converge has yielded a critical finding for proximal composite optimization: under a Lipschitz-assumption on the outer composite function, it can be assumed that consecutive iterates converge exponentially. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating an environment simulator to facilitate automatic skill acquisition through human demonstration. However, various realistic environments pose challenges due to dynamic settings, untimed actions, and multiple possible paths to a goal. To overcome these obstacles, we propose the Cross-Area Imitation from Observations (CAIO) framework, designed to learn diverse skills across different settings using only recorded human demonstrations. The framework leverages observations common to all skill areas to establish a universal representation, facilitating the development of condition-free policies. The CAIO framework comprises three key components: representation learning, policy learning, and area weighting, working in tandem to enhance the imitation performance of our method when applied to various reinforcement learning problems. The representation learning module uses the shared observations to create a general skill repository, while area weighting determines the likelihood of applying a learned skill in different settings. The policy learning module achieves low-level policies to enrich the skill repository. The framework can be viewed as discovering a graph, where nodes represent skills and edges define the conditions for applying one skill to another. We evaluated our approach using diverse skill areas in multiple reinforcement learning tasks and found that CAIO consistently outperforms existing imitation methods, ultimately demonstrating the potential of CAIO for automatic skill acquisition through human demonstration across various realistic environments. A major uncertainty in calculating the initial stellar masses of the first generation of stars, which were formed in the early universe, is due to a lack of clarity around how the intensification of magnetic fields influence the disk fragmentation in these stars. In order to investigate this, we simulated the formation of a protostar and its surrounding disk using advanced software and assumed the presence of amplified magnetic fields. Our simulation revealed that highly turbulent and dense disk areas were fragmented in the absence of magnetic effects, but when we accounted for the guidance of magnetic fields, all forms of fragmentation were eliminated. This suggests that highly turbulent and dense regions of protostellar disks may not fragment due to magnetic effects, which in turn could influence the initial stellar mass range of the first generation of stars. Additionally, our findings may also explain why compact and high-mass stars are relatively rare in the early universe. Mental illness plays a substantial role in the criminal justice system, with research indicating that roughly half of prisoners possess some form of mental disorder. This is particularly evident among inmates undergoing treatment within the United States, where approximately 25% of prisoners are engaged in some type of therapy. Notably, studies have shown that mental illnesses are significantly underdiagned and undertreated within this population. In an effort to address this critical issue, some jurisdictions are making mental health services compulsory for prisoners upon release from correctional facilities. Although this policy seeks to enhance mental health outcomes among this vulnerable demographic, concerns persist regarding its efficacy due to varying research methodologies and treatment models. Our analysis suggests that requiring therapy leads to an increase in the percentage of individuals receiving mental health services, and also results in improved mental health outcomes among this population, as evidenced by lower symptom counts. Notably, our findings indicate that the effectiveness of mandatory therapy depends on the length of the required treatment period, with larger effects observed among participants undergoing longer periods of therapy. Our research also reveals that mandatory therapy has a more pronounced effect on improved mental health outcomes among prisoners receiving some form of therapy prior to their conviction, as well as those undergoing treatment for anxiety and depression. Conversely, we discover that mandatory therapy lacks a statistically significant effect on symptoms among prisoners undergoing treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder. Federated learning allows a centralized server to collectively train a global model by aggregating contributions from user devices, typically with synchronized gradient updates, but this can lead to slow convergence due to waiting for all devices to report their gradients, or poor model performance through data imbalance. To resolve these limitations, researchers have explored asynchrony, either in gradient updates or accumulation, but this often necessitates devices waiting for each other and/or the server to combine their gradients, thereby reducing efficiency. To address these challenges, we introduce FedBA, a novel FL protocol that enables the efficient combination of asynchronous gradient updates and collective model waiting. FedBA utilizes the server buffering all device gradients and accumulates them asynchronously, then aggregates and applies the aggregated gradient when communication is complete, while also providing several optimizations to enhance performance. Specifically, we introduce gradient clipping, normalized stabilization, and adaptive waiting policies to promote faster convergence and reduce model instability. Our experiments validate FedBA's superior efficiency and performance compared to existing FL protocols in synthetic and real-world tests. Additionally, we observe FedBA's training dynamics, which differ from conventional FL, and note its potential for improved model generalization. A raft is a flat structure consisting of a rigid base and flexible membranes that separate its compartments. This research investigates the breakdown of rafts with multiple compartments under various loading conditions. Additionally, the study considers the scenario where fluids within the compartments have different densities, which introduces an additional mechanism of collapse through density instability. This analysis applies both to isotropic and anisotropic raft structures and predicts the shape of cracks in specific density configurations. Finally, the study explores the impact of fractures on carrying capacity and reveals a relationship between the number of fractures and this capacity. It also observes the behavior of system components during rupture and notes their variation due to the presence of fractures. This research expects to contribute to a deeper understanding of raft failure and its applications in modeling flat structures. It also enables the use of raft failure as a model to study other physical systems that exhibit similar types of breakdown. This note examines robust shift equivalence in the context of row-finite graphs and their associated C*-algebras, particularly AΓ. We reevaluate the definition of robust shift equivalence, aiming to eliminate unnecessary assumptions and establish a more general concept. This new concept is grounded in the idea that a pair of paths connecting two vertices in a graph should be shift equivalent, regardless of the vertices' choice. This broader definition encompasses notable instances, such as infinite path graphs and directed trees. However, it contradicts another significant theorem, leading to the conclusion that the set of robust shift equivalent classes is not necessarily categorical. This result implies the presence of non-trivial invariants for shift equivalent graphs, allowing for their differentiation. Consequently, we develop a new invariant, which aids in determining the uniqueness of the C*-algebraic shift action for a graph, thereby supplementing existing criteria. Finally, we investigate the uniqueness of the C*-algebraic shift action for graphs with at most three edges in a given direction. Additionally, we demonstrate that the C*-algebraic shift action is unique for graphs lacking edges in a single direction and possessing at most three edges in an opposite direction. This finding broadens an existing criterion for trees with additional restrictions. Moreover, we present an example illustrating a non-trivial instance of shift equivalent graphs with a unique C*-algebraic shift action, thereby addressing unanswered questions in the field. Notably, we leave the resolution of the shift equivalent classes in graphs with at most three edges in a given direction unanswered. This problem has significant implications for understanding the C*-algebraic shift action and mapping it to a universal C*-algebra. Therefore, determining the shift equivalent classes in graphs with at most three edges in a given direction may yield valuable insights into the universal C*-algebra and the mapping of its shift action. This, in turn, could facilitate a more comprehensive investigation into the universal C*-algebraic shift action, ultimately allowing for a more in-depth analysis of its associated algebra. This line of inquiry may lead to advances in the field and enhance our understanding of the underlying physics. Furthermore, resolving this problem could enhance our knowledge of graph shift equivalent classes and exploit their mapping to the universal C*-algebra. This, in turn, could foster a more general understanding of the universal C*-algebra and the graph shift action. Meanwhile, we examined the one-way connected graphs and discovered that the shift equivalent classes in graphs with at least three edges in a given direction can be exhaustively characterised.

Our study evaluates a range of factors influencing prompt effectiveness, including language style, length, complexity, and degree of specification, all in a zero-shot setting involving text-classification and multiple-choice tasks through the crowdsource platform Crowdsourcing Platform. We discovered substantial variability in prompt performance, with certain types achieving significantly higher levels of accuracy than others. Our top-performing prompt style resulted in a 72% overall success rate, representing a substantial enhancement (of 21%) over our baseline prompt. Our pre-trained language model, fine-tuned on informative data, demonstrated superior robustness in the presence of ambiguous data and prompt imperfections. Our investigation provides quantitative insights to guide the design of prompts in a wide range of applications, while also highlighting potential biases in the types of choices requested in existing datasets. Our code and dataset are accessible for reproduction at this location: Repository. Additionally, we find an expression for the topological Leopoldt $\mathscr{L}$-invariant of any Artin motive, which expresses it in terms of the finite, $\mathbb{Q}_{\infty}$-finitely generated motive $\mathrm{Mot}^{Fus}_{\mathrm{tor}}$. This enables us to relate the Leopoldt $\mathscr{L}$-invariant of a number field $K$ to its Galois group $G_K$ and the fusion map $\Phi_{G_K}: \mathrm{Mot}^{Fus}_{\mathrm{tor}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mot}_{G_K}$. Identifying the atomic Rydberg states is crucial for developing precise microwave sensing technologies. Conventional approaches utilizing autoionizing states have limitations due to the challenges of working with these highly excited atoms. Our research overcomes these limitations through the implementation of a novel deep neural network called Rydberg Identification through Deep learning for Multifrequency microwave detection. This model leverages the features of autoionizing states and Rydberg states, enhancing Rydberg state detection, as evidenced by a significant boost in performance, from 70% to 93%, using only 1000 training examples. Furthermore, it demonstrates increased resilience to noise, as validated by experiments and simulations, making it an effective method for identifying Rydberg states in diverse atomic systems. Its accessibility via a web-based interface allows for easy model access and sharing. Our work sets a new standard for Rydberg state detection and enters the list of top performing teams in the 2021 DeepLearning@Home challenge. This achievement is notable as the new method outperforms existing approaches when evaluating only the new submissions from the challenge website. Our model is currently available online, with the source code and data, at this repository. UGC 8839, an extremely faint spiral galaxy, possesses an remarkable circular structure. The exceptional clarity of Hubble Space Telescope images reveal a well-defined, undisturbed disk formed primarily of young, blue-starforming regions. The seamless integration of the central structure to the main disk suggests there has been no recent minor merger affecting the galaxy's appearance. Contrasting to most spiral galaxies displaying starforming regions at their edges, UGC 8839's starsforming regions predominantly face towards the center due to the relatively strong central bulge relative to its overall mass. The relatively small overall mass of the galaxy, estimated to be approximately 2.4 x 10^9 solar masses, means it has not experienced the necessary gravitational forces from an interacting object to explain the unusual circular pattern of starforming regions.

The unique spiral pattern of UGC 8839, resembling a ring with its hub, could be the result of a supernova that collapsed the galaxy's core, causing material to spiral inwards in the center while young starforming regions in the outer regions maintain their original rotational velocity. This exceptional structure, visible in the Hubble Space Telescope images, marks the first instance of a 'hyper-constant' disk pattern in a spiral galaxy. This unique pattern, visible from afar, might serve as an indicator for a supernova's significant impact on a galaxy's evolution and could potentially explain various unusual features in spiral galaxies that have not been resolved by current observations. Further studies are needed to verify whether this remarkable structure is shared by other spiral galaxies. If so, it could offer valuable insights into the significant effects a supernova explosion can have on a galaxy's overall structure and evolution.

A method to generate sound in real-time by linking images to audio spectra is developed, allowing for the creation of visually guided sound effects. A database of image-to-audio mappings is created using deep neural networks, which can be used to produce synthetic sounds from visual inputs. This technique is contingent on having access to a large dataset of labeled sound images, as well as an understanding of the visual cues that correlate with the desired audio outcomes. Research demonstrates the efficacy of this approach, albeit with limitations: the quality of synthesized sounds is highly dependent on the size of the dataset, and distinct visual elements can be utilized to control the frequency or timbre of the generated sounds. Future developments could entail expanding the scope to video-to-audio synthesis and the creation of more intricate sound effects. A software application based on this research is available for public use at https://github.com/magenta/reverb. A corresponding YouTube video showcasing the capabilities can be found at https://youtu.be/6m8T4QF_1GQ. Important discussions took place at Stanford University, New York University, and University of Oregon. This is achieved by leveraging multiple sequential inputs, effectively creating a temporal hierarchy within the networks. In contrast, conventional architectures lacking recurrent connections fail to acquire temporal sequencing, as shown by identical outcomes from experiments conducted on multiple tasks. Additionally, our findings emphasize the significance of sequential ordering in hierarchical temporal representations, as well as highlight the difficulties encountered when attempting to incorporate temporal knowledge into flat architectures. To find a pandemic mitigation strategy that balances health and economic outcomes, we compared various timelines for implementing non-pharmaceutical interventions in a basic economic model of disease transmission. The results show that delaying these interventions until after the pandemic peak yields worse outcomes than imposing them early, as this approach amplifies the total infection rate, hospitalization counts, mortality toll, and overall economic devastation. In contrast, timely interventions, whether introduced early or late, produce remarkably similar outcomes in both health and economic metrics, regardless of the pandemic's severity. The disparity in performance is most pronounced when the difference in intervention timelines is large, with smaller discrepancies producing gradually diminishing variations in outcomes. The economic benefits of early interventions are largely attributed to lower costs associated with fewer hospitalizations and fatalities. The optimal timing of non-pharmaceutical interventions is not only context-sensitive but also depends on the specific countermeasure used, whereas the universal solution of acting promptly applies to all countermeasures. The findings of our analysis align with recent empirical observations suggesting that some countries, which implemented non-pharmaceutical interventions early in the pandemic, experienced lower death rates and economic losses than those that acted later. Conversely, other nations' examples highlight the potential drawbacks of premature easing of restrictions, demonstrating the potential for revived infection surges, hospital overloads, and severe economic consequences. Ultimately, the widespread applicability of our discovery of early intervention efficacy to various countermeasures underscores the importance of timing in the implementation of disease transmission mitigation strategies. The findings of our study also highlight ongoing disparities in outcomes resulting from differences in the timing of interventions, underscoring the need for further action to address these inequalities. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that disease transmission models involving fundamental countermeasure transmission patterns may be adequate for capturing the effects of different intervention timelines, implying a reasonable level of simplicity and universality in modeling the countermeasures themselves. The potential limitations of our study are briefly addressed, and areas for further research are also mentioned. The effectiveness of machine learning applications can be compromised by issues arising from data quality problems. However, pinpointing the root cause of these problems is a complex task, mainly because data quality defects can span the entire data preprocessing pipeline and are difficult to replicate. The concept of influence, a measure used to assess the impact of data records on model performance, is introduced, along with a framework for tracking changes in influence throughout the pipeline. The framework ultimately enables the identification of problematic data records based on their combined influence contribution, denoted as Shapley significance. Practical demonstrations utilizing real-world datasets have shown the efficacy of this approach in data quality troubleshooting. Furthermore, this work presents a new metric, end-to-end Shapley significance, to evaluate the overall impact of data records on the machine learning pipeline. By utilizing this metric under a optimisation paradigm, data records with the greatest impact can be selectively removed to improve model performance, effectively triggering a search for their underlying cause. The proposed approach is grounded in two theoretical findings that establish its validity and optimality. The integration of this work's ideas into modern data analytics systems is suggested, enabling proactive data quality maintenance and optimising the quality of the data used to train and evaluate models. Experimental results, including those presented at the 2021 Shapley AI Workshop, have shown the efficacy of this approach in machine learning and its potential to improve model performance by detecting and removing problematic data records. The novel end-to-end Shapley significance metric holds potential applications in fields such as bioinformatics and auditing, where data quality maintenance may yield substantial financial gains. A demonstration is offered on GitHub, allowing users to replicate the results and showcase the versatility of this concept, which can be applied to a wide range of data and machine learning scenarios. Users can modify and customise the code to suit their specific needs and explore the influence tracking framework in conjunction with machine learning libraries such as scikit-learn and TensorFlow. The integration of this concept into production data analytics systems is envisioned, ultimately leading to proactive data quality maintenance and optimised results. The data records with Shapley significance can be used to train and evaluate models, ultimately yielding better performance. A theoretical examination of optimisation paradigms is presented, along with several experimental findings, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in machine learning and its potential to improve model results. The novel end-to-end Shapley significance metric holds promise for various data quality maintenance applications. A data trove containing problem data is offered on GitHub, allowing users to replicate the results and showcase the versatility

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. A pressure range of 0-30 GPa causes a significant decrease in the anomalous Hall resistance, with a notable drop-off around 15 GPa. Crystal growth studies reveal that this pressure threshold is correlated with a structural transformation within the material, specifically the transition from a low-pressure hexagonal phase to a high-pressure tetragonal phase. To further investigate this correlation, we conducted a comprehensive computational analysis, incorporating both first-principles calculations and classical Monte Carlo simulations to examine the relationship between pressure, spin waves, and lattice distortion in Mn$_3$Sn. Our computational model accurately replicates the experimentally observed changes, attributing the Anomalous Hall effect suppression to the pressure-driven destruction of easy-axis magnetic domains through spin wave scattering. Our research provides a greater understanding of the interplay between symmetry, electron transport, and spin waves in Mn$_3$Sn, offering insights into the optimal design of antiferromagnetic materials with enhanced electronic properties. Additionally, we have expanded the computational model to investigate the physical properties of superconducting Mn$_3$Sn and tritanide compounds. Our analysis paves the way for the design and development of novel antiferromagnetic and superconducting materials using a unified framework, as the achieved tetragonal structure under high pressure in Mn$_3$Sn reveals a potential pathway to stabilize a long-elusive long-range bond in this class of materials. Furthermore, our research suggests that high-pressure synthesis could facilitate the creation of novel states in momentum space, enabling the realization of magnetic topological insulators and Weyl semimetals, as well as superconductors with unusual symmetry characteristics. Our study offers a groundbreaking perspective on the utilization of external pressures to engineer unique quantum states in materials. Additionally, our research provides a framework for the systematic analysis of pressure-dependent phase diagrams in magnetic and superconducting materials, with the potential to uncover previously unknown phases and transitions. Our findings demonstrate that high-pressure experiments, combined with computational modeling, can significantly contribute to the discovery of novel materials with unique properties. Improving the accuracy of out-of-domain testing is a crucial challenge for explaining how a machine learning model works. We address this issue by examining the impact of data transformations on neural networks. These data transformations artificially alter a model's perception of its input data, often resulting in decreased accuracy. We investigate whether these transformations can reveal network weaknesses and enhance the accuracy of other machine learning models. We focus on precision medicine, specifically the prediction of breast cancer subtypes, and investigate whether certain data transformations can improve network generalization. We examine the potential of guided network reconstruction, which involves incorporating specific patterns into the model's internal structures, as a means of enhancing accuracy. We explore various guided reconstruction methods, analyzing their effectiveness and examining their impact when applied to multiple datasets. However, these experiments indicate that guided reconstruction does not consistently improve accuracy, and we suggest hybridizing it with other forms of network compression to create guided hypergraph reconstruction. This novel approach involves expanding the model's internal structures while maintaining a reduced overall topology. We test this method on the task of predicting breast cancer subtypes, as well as on image classification, and find that it provides more consistent and substantial accuracy improvements. We provide code for this project at https://github.com/bk-39/guided-hypergraph-reconstruction. A method to estimate a shear-thickening or shear-thinning fluid's viscosity from cross-coralation measurements in a layered flow setup is developed and investigated. The estimation technique employs physical optics principles and assumes a two-layer flow scenario with constant viscosity profiles and parallel velocity directions. The viscosity of each layer is calculated by analyzing the cross-coralation measurements in cross-stream and streamwise directions using a Fourier domain approach. The effectiveness of this estimation method is validated through comprehensive numerical simulations, which demonstrate its ability to accurately determine both layers' viscosities even when the underlying assumptions are slightly violated. Notably, the study finds that the estimation method performs exceptionally well when the Saffman boundary layer is present, albeit slightly biased for shear-thinning fluids. Conversely, the incorporation of a shear band into the shear-thinning layer yields improved estimates, outperforming those from the shear-thickening case. Ultimately, the research concludes that the proposed estimation method yields precise and accurate results for layer-parallel cross-coralation measurements, particularly in cases involving shear-thinning fluids with a shear band. The estimated viscosities exhibit minimal differences from the actual values, with average errors less than 0.1% for the inner layer and 0.3% for the outer layer. The proposed estimation method is deemed suitable for a range of applications, with potential expansions to various topics in geophysics and geology. The study recommends conducting further exploration into the application and extension of physical optics techniques in geophysical fluid dynamics. Additionally, the research offers an estimated lower bound for the Prandtl number in layered shear flows. The study presents novel insights into the self-similar nature of these flows, shedding light on the behavior of layered shear flows with adjacent fluids of significantly differing viscosities. The research is anticipated to contribute to the development of novel estimation methods for viscous fluids based on cross-coralation measurements. The estimated viscosities or viscosivity ratios can be further utilized in elucidating many geophysical and geological phenomena, such as turbidity current modeling, mantle convection, and multilayer fluid dynamics. We test this method on a range of artificial configurations and find that it effectively identifies all the biased divisions it's trained on, as well as some additional unfair configurations. This idea can be expanded to tackle various conceptually related problems. As virtual agents navigate these text-based environments, they encounter challenges similar to those faced by humans in interactive stories. Current models can process and respond to text inputs in approximately 100 to 1000 times per second. In contrast, humans can process approximately 40 words per second when reading text. This discrepancy suggests the need for more advanced models. This paper presents TextWorldExpress, an artificial intelligence that can process and respond to text inputs in approximately one million times per second. TextWorldExpress achieves this level of efficiency through the integration of several innovations, including the incorporation of pre-trained language models, the utilization of compressed game representations, and the implementation of elevated-level reasoning strategies. As a result, TextWorldExpress can complete text-based games at a speed 10 to 100 times faster than alternative models. These events, which affect multiple geographical locations at once, are challenging to identify and analyze. Our work introduces a novel method to capture simultaneous extreme situations in the Gulf of Mexico by leveraging a unified framework that targets rare combinations of spatial patterns. This approach utilizes Markov Random Fields to model the joint occurrence of extreme values in multiple locations, and then develops a statistical measure that highlights areas experiencing the most severe conditions. Our results reveal that the proposed method significantly outperforms traditional techniques based on thresholding and clustering, by accurately detecting the most critical multiple-site extreme events and characterizing their temporal variations in the Gulf of Mexico during the summer months. This research demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method for applications involving multiple variables, as well as its ease of implementation and efficient computational performance. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of persistent marine extremes and highlight the importance of further research in this field. Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of nonconstant meromorphic functions over number fields, extending previous results by Druel, Weymann, and Xarouts. Specifically, we demonstrate that a general nonconstant meromorphic function on a smooth projective variety over a number field has a finite set of rational zeros. Furthermore, we show that under an assumption of nondegenerate fibers, such a function is actually morphically finite, meaning it has a bounded number of zeros given a fixed degree of singularity. When we relax the nondegeneracy assumption, we prove that the number of rational zeros is indeed bounded under certain conditions on the singularities, thus resolving a question posed by Xarouts. Lastly, we speculate that the removal of singularities criterion could be replaced by a simpler condition based on arithmetic equivalence, which would yield the same result. Ultimately, our research suggests the plausibility of an unconditional application of Arakelov-Jouanna theorem. Additionally, our work relates to Green's theorem and our analysis explores various boundary cases, shedding light on the interplay between algebraic and analytic geometry. Lastly, our investigation examines the particular case of functions with few singularities, yielding conclusions on the number of rational zeros based on degree and Picard number. Ultimately, our study suggests the rational zeros could be counted by counting the entire zeros, provided the degree exceeds the square root of the Picard number. In fact, our results can be extended to nonhyperbolic projective varieties, such as abelian varieties and varieties with ample line bundles. We utilize a combination of arithmetic algebraic geometry, including Faltings' theorem and the arithmetic Monge-Ampere theorem, as well as analytical methods, including removable singularity theoreorems and the Rouche theorem. By integrating these approaches, we examine the extent to which nonconstant meromorphic functions on nonhyperbolic projective varieties exhibit analytic properties, thereby connecting arithmetic algebraic geometry to complex analytic geometry. We also explore various quantitative applications and consider several explicit case studies, such as the family of elliptic curves, the quintic elliptic surface, and other notable varieties, thereby illustrating our theoreorems with numerous examples and highlighting the intricate connections between algebraic and analytic geometry. A key issue in operating complex robots with precise pose accuracy is human operability. To address this, we've developed a system for adapting task spaces to improve human-robot interaction. Essentially, this system aligns the robot's motion control space with the human's natural movement dynamics. Our method involves using a non-linear optimization framework, which utilizes a specialized algorithm based on Information-Filtering Iterative Closest Point. This algorithm efficiently maps human hand movements to a stable, efficient robot motion control space, even in environments with occlusions and human hand motion ambiguities. Testing on a Gantry robot demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, which resulting in improved human-robot interaction and reduced task completion time. Additionally, the proposed method shows promise for use with other complex robots. A video showcasing the system in action can be found here: https://youtu.be/7s4TO3R9ylM. Furthermore, the developed methodology is capable of transferring knowledge between different robots and tasks, which is illustrated by transferring a motion control space from a UR10 to an XtremePuma260 robot. This capability known as multi-domain adaptation, significantly expands the potential applications and benefits of our method. A significant aspect of our work is that it is compliant with both human and robotic safety regulations, due to its data-driven and data-normalization features. To facilitate the replication of our results, we've made available the proposed method, as well as the necessary data set containing human hand motion captured via high-resolution RGB-D cameras, via this GitHub repository: https://github.com/RobotLearning/HRDAD. Our work presents an innovative solution for efficiently mapping human hand motion to robot motion control spaces, which is crucial for enhancing human-robot interaction and is applicable across a range of complex robots and tasks. This method involves comparing the predicted matrix elements of signal and background events to those measured experimentally. A common challenge in real-world robotics is determining the 3D positional coordinates of an object. Typically, this is achieved through the use of special sensors, but in real-life situations these sensors can be expensive, unreliable, or simply not available. A possible solution to this problem is to train a robot to determine an object's 3D coordinates by observing its movement if it is placed on a plane and caused to rotate. This paper presents an approach to training a robot to achieve this goal, which we refer to as observing unintentional turntables (OUT). An OUT scenario is defined as a situation in which an object's rotation is not intentionally caused by the robot for the purpose of data collection. This approach can be applied to objects with any shape and is suitable for robots operating in environments where accurate 3D object modeling is required. An evaluation pipeline is developed to assess the accuracy of the trained model in determining 3D positional coordinates on unseen objects and scenes. The results of numerous experiments conducted using diverse datasets reveal that the trained models are capable of accurately positioning objects regardless of their type, pose, and number of visible features. Crucially, the accuracy of the models is found to be highest when training involves a large collection of diverse objects rather than a limited range of objects. This capability makes the proposed approach highly versatile and suitable for a range of real-world tasks. An open-source package providing detailed information about the approach as well as demonstration videos are available online. This work represents the first documented application of deep learning to determine 3D object positioning through observation of objects rotating on a plane. As a result, the proposed approach has the potential to broaden the scope of deep learning applications in robotics and 3D object modeling. Furthermore, the trained models can be utilized in a variety of other tasks such as 3D object recognition, sorting, and categorization. An area of further exploration could involve incorporating the observed rotation movements to enhance the accuracy of object positioning and feature estimation. Additionally, the integration of the proposed approach with existing 3D object perception methods could potentially lead to the development of a more robust and accurate decision-making system capable of utilizing multiple sources of information to determine 3D object positioning.
