The rapid dissemination of incomplete and inaccurate information regarding COVID-19 vaccines is threatening the public's perception of vaccine efficacy. Social media platforms are breeding grounds for misinformation, as users engage in online conversations that influence each other's beliefs. Existing misinformation detection systems typically rely on automated techniques that analyze digital content, but often fall short by overlooking context and individual perspectives. Conversely, manual or semi-automated methods, such as crowdsourcing or expert analysis, can consider various factors, but are often impractical due to scalability issues. This study proposes a novel approach that leverages advanced natural language processing and machine learning techniques to capture content, social influence, and individual perspectives within online conversations. We evaluated this method by designing a novel dataset consisting of Twitter dialogue exchanges related to COVID-19 vaccines, where users' interactions are examined to determine the acceptance or rejection of misinformation. The proposed system achieved a competitive performance of 0.88 F1-score on an experimental dataset that was generated through an efficient process utilizing automated and human verification techniques. Notably, our study acknowledges the inherent limitations of online content labeling and discusses the potential implications for misinformation detection and discrete content analysis. The proposed algorithm and dataset are jointly designed to address the distinct challenges of predicting acceptance or rejection of misinformation and understanding discrete content, respectively. This research contributes to these areas by developing a novel content representation and an acceptance/rejection prediction model, as well as a unique dataset that incorporates human perspectives and social influence. We anticipate that our work will facilitate the exploration of novel approaches to misinformation detection and understanding, where social media content goes beyond mere information and is inherently conversational. The proposed model and dataset are publicly accessible for replication purposes. The Twitter dialogue dataset can be accessed via https://github.com/nyu-fall-2020-nyu-ai-20291003/COVID-Vaccine-Twitter-Dialogue/tree/main/data. The code for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/nyu-fall-2020-nyu-ai-20291003/COVID-Vaccine-Tweet-Classification. The manipulation of high-energy, attosecond pulses in the vicinity of strong, inhomogeneous electric fields poses significant challenges, yet offers the potential to greatly increase our control over pulse generation and its output energy. To address these difficulties, we develop a theoretical framework based on a density matrix approach, enabling the consistent description of pulse evolution in the presence of strong, position-dependent electric fields and the resulting non-equilibrium electronic dynamics. This framework, called the Multi-Directional High-Harmonic Generation (MDDHG) model, demonstrates the robustness of controlling attosecond pulses over a wide range of scenarios, including irregular laser focuses and particles positioned at arbitrary angles with respect to the polarization plane. This allows for enhanced pulse generation and energy optimization, while also offering new insights into the MDCS phenomenon itself. The MDDHG model provides an efficient tool to explore the vast potential of coherent pulse manipulation. The findings of our research can be applied to enhance pulse characteristics in many current and future tabletop experiments focused on attosecond science, and it may also be adapted for other applications such as attosecond metrology and nonlinear spectroscopy. The detection of binary stars at birth is significant because their formation processes offer insights into the overall star formation rate at that moment. Recent studies using data from the Spitzer Space Telescope claimed the presence of a new member in the Algol family, a triple star system known as Algol (beta Persei). This study presents high-resolution infrared observations of Algol and a surrounding area, collected over eight years, starting from 2006, as part of the Spitzer Legacy Program. It analyzed infrared data of the system, but couldn't verify the existence of the proposed companion object. Instead, the observations confidently detected the system's two established members, revealing their properties and confirming their distances from the bright star. This data ruled out the possibility of a faint companion object that could have been mistaken for a background source. An examination of the solved triple system's dynamics, using data from high-resolution and infrared observations, confirmed that the system is dynamically relaxed and consistent with their distances from the bright star. This means that the formation of Algol's members, including its relatively close companion, must have occurred far away from the bright star, rather than through a exchange as part of a higher order system as initially suggested. Our findings join a group of similar discoveries that refute recently made proposals of fresh companions within well-known multiple star systems. These findings could imply that the exchange of material between stars is less common than expected, particularly at close ranges. An alternative explanation for the anomaly of Algol's configuration also is discussed, including the possibility of gaining excessive mass by its closest companion thanks to the dynamic interaction of the system as a whole, thus achieving an unusual distance from the bright star without participating in a higher order structure. Despite displaying accuracy on equilibrium problems, further developments are needed to effectively tackle time-dependent equations. This involves creating additional vertices on the network's layer structure to process inputs, allowing for the efficient use of physics-informed constraints on the output. However, this results in increased parameters and complexity. To mitigate these issues, a new adaptive vertex creation method, referred to as Residual-based Adaptive NGrounds, was introduced. This method creates vertices dynamically based on the smoothness of error estimates generated from residual error. Additionally, the method is adaptable to various loss functions and datasets, making it a versatile tool for solving differential equations. This study examines the behavior and modeling of FeFETs that comprise multiple domains separated by domain wall states, which significantly increase the device's capacitance due to a substantial increase in the dielectric constant near the walls. Unlike traditional FeFETs, where the channel is solely made up of the ferroelectric component, these multi-domain devices involve a complex mixture of ferroelectric and paraelectric regions. As the device's capacitance is directly linked to the time it takes for domain switching to occur, this novel capacitance phenomenon emerges at very short timescales. We develop a simulation framework that effectively models the cross-capacitance phenomenon observed in these devices and explores how it relates to the switching speed of the ferroelectric material. This novel device behavior is likely to have a substantial impact on steep-slope logic design and may necessitate the development of new design strategies. This work is the first to explore the fundamental relationship between Trojan assaults and semantic modifications, opening doors for future research. Achieving ambiguity reduction is a fundamental objective in various scientific studies across biology, medicine, pharmacology, and physics. In the context of machine learning, addressing ambiguity is crucial for enhancing model performance and generalizability. Although several ambiguity reduction techniques have been proposed and applied in different scientific contexts, a comprehensive review and comparison of these methods is currently lacking. To bridge this knowledge gap, we conduct an in-depth analysis of commonly employed ambiguity reduction techniques, utilized in both supervised and unsupervised settings, utilizing numerical simulations and case studies from different scientific domains. Our work specifically explores taxonomy, performance evaluation, and illustrative examples of uncertainty quantification, clustering, and classification techniques aimed at reducing ambiguity. These ambient-driven machine learning approaches are highly relevant to scientists tackling challenges in systems biology, personalized medicine, drug discovery, and astrophysics. Our study utilizes numerical experiments and case studies involving real-world data from bird sound classification, forest cover-type mapping, cancer risk assessment, and galaxy classification to evaluate the performance of these ambiguity reduction techniques. Our work compares and contrasts different ambiguity reduction methods, highlighting their advantages and limitations to guide practitioners in selecting the most suitable approaches for addressing ambiguity in diverse scientific contexts. These analyses also uncover opportunities for incorporating uncertainty estimation and clustering methods into deep learning paradigms, ultimately facilitating ambiguity reduction. Our study ultimately establishes a framework for evaluating ambiguity reduction techniques and their potential applications across various scientific domains. It remains to be seen how ambiguity analysis will evolve in the context of causal machine learning, which may offer novel, domain-specific approaches. It is conceivable that future advancements in this field will yield surprise hits, much like how recurrent neural networks and convolutional neural networks were unexpected breakthroughs. These potential breakthroughs could potentially integrate domain-specific ambiguity reduction techniques with existing machine learning approaches, thereby leveraging their respective strengths. It is also conceivable that future advancements will utilize various scientific contexts to address challenges in causal machine learning, thereby incorporating domain-specific ambiguity reduction techniques. These potential breakthroughs could potentially surprise experts in machine learning. The study provides a comprehensive review and comparison of commonly employed ambiguity reduction techniques, addressing supervised and unsupervised settings, utilizing numerical experiments and case studies from different scientific domains. The numerical analysis evaluates and compares the performance of these techniques, highlighting their applications and limitations to guide practitioners in addressing ambiguity across various scientific contexts. The comparative study assesses uncertainty quantification, clustering, and classification methods aimed at reducing ambiguity, ultimately establishing a framework for evaluating these techniques and their potential uses in diverse scientific domains. When dealing with large-scale Markov Decision Processes, solving the Bellman Equation often presents a significant challenge. This article focuses on estimating the optimal value function using an iterative algorithm based on the Generalized Minimum Residual method. This approach is modified to handle approximations and is implemented with an automatic termination condition tied to the accuracy of the approximation. Experiments are conducted to compare its performance with other methods, including neural network-based approximation methods, on a range of problems. Notably, the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of computational efficiency while achieving comparable levels of policy accuracy. Ultimately, this method is found to be a viable option for obtaining precise value function estimates when high-precision estimates are required. This article is self-contained, providing all necessary details for the algorithm and used terminology. Two supplementary materials contain additional information: a package for conducting the presented experiments and a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed graphs known as directed paths. Furthermore, the study also identifies both a necessary and a sufficient condition under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ exhibit equal behavior. To support our findings, specific classes of weighted directed trees and directed cycles are analyzed to provide illustrative examples. We also investigate the depth of edge ideals resulting from weighted directed trees and establish a connection with the number of vertices in the underlying graph. Specifically, our examples demonstrate that the depth of $I(\mathcal{D})$ can increase as the edge multiplicity decreases, thereby extending previous works of Sbarra and El Khoury as cited in the study. Additionally, our research provides answers to previously posed questions of Hemasathya and White as cited in the study. We also introduce the concept of strong connectedness in weighted directed graphs, particularly weighted directed trees, and show its significance through the relation it fosters with the depth of their edge ideals. To summarize, our research offers a comprehensive exploration into which weighted directed graphs have an edge ideal that exhibits equal symbolic and ordinary power series. Although our study focuses on weighted directed graphs, the concepts of strong connectedness and edge ideals can also be applied to undirected graphs to yield complementary results. We also outline potential future research directions and possible questions that arise from the themes discussed in the study. Moreover, our examples in the text illustrate how the ideas presented can be applied to real-world scenarios of directed graphs. We also discuss how our research on edge ideals can also be referred to as lexicographic shellability in the context of directed graphs. The process of modeling complex systems using computer simulation often relies on identifying the appropriate model through reverse engineering, where observed time series data is matched to a theoretical model. In this study, we explore this inverse problem in the context of queueing models, seeking to estimate key distribution parameters based on sample paths of a queueing network. Due to the non-differentiable and complex nature of time series data, along with the high dimensionality of parameter spaces, a conventional least squares approach is impractical. Instead, we propose a multiple contours of influence estimator utilizing non-parametric kernel density methods to smooth time series data, thereby simplifying the inverse problem. This proposed estimator is demonstrated to be consistent under specific conditions and performs well in practical applications, as evidenced by our analysis of its robustness to contamination and empirical results illustrating its effectiveness in resolving the inverse problem. Additionally, we discuss the applicability of this approach to integrating simulation model validation with model reduction, enabling the identification of appropriate representations for complex queueing networks. Our contribution offers a versatile solution to addressing the inverse problem in computer simulation, with relevant implications extending beyond queueing theory to the broader field of complex system modeling. This includes applications such as modeling population dynamics, understanding historical events based on testimonies, and interpreting scientific or clinical data. To gauge a network's connectivity and a node's influence within it, researchers have employed various centrality measures. In the context of resilient learning, where multiple distributed learners collaborate and a fraction of them can be compromised by adversaries, measuring network connectivity helps learners gauge the likelihood of their counterparts' integrity. A small number of these measures, such as degree centrality, effectively capture this likelihood; the rest, including closeness and betweenness centrality, are sensitive to attacks and thus unreliable. A new centralization measure, dubbed the resilience centralization measure, is introduced to evaluate a network's connectivity and individual node importance under adversarial manipulation. This measure proves useful in ascertaining the helpfulness of regional queries in enhancing learning robustness. Specifically, it demonstrates that: (1) regional aggregates are always beneficial when multiple neighboring learners collaborate; (2) regional aggregates are occasionally beneficial in various distributed learning settings, but often fail to surpass standalone training; (3) regional aggregates are invariably beneficial in enhancing robustness, but generally do not surpass standalone training; (4) regional aggregates are occasionally detrimental when adversaries specifically target nodes with high regional importance outside one's immediate neighborhood; (5) regional aggregates are beneficial in settings involving constant admission of new learners and can significantly boost robustness in such scenarios. This research offers insight into the usefulness of regional queries in various distributed learning environments and this implementation is made available on GitHub. Furthermore, three additional test environments, comprising non-stationary, directed, and dynamic networks, are provided alongside code and data. Results show that regional queries remain beneficial in non-stationary scenarios but are occasionally beneficial in directed graphs and generally unnecessary in dynamic networks where periodical node admission suffices. This research presents a novel perspective on centrality in the context of distributed learning and resilient networks. Two key concepts, individual and system importance, emerge from this research. Firstly, a node's individual importance refers to its inherent value within the network; secondly, a system's importance represents its overall robustness and centralization. This distinction is significant, as it partakes in distributed learning and resilient training respectively. Developing robust models in such collaborative learning environments necessitates evaluating both individual and system importance. Results demonstrate that centralization is a critical factor driving robustness and centralization scores are also predictive of learner and node integrity in distributed and network-based training. In this study, the production rates of various particles, including pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons, were measured in midrapidity during Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV. Particle yields are examined as a function of centrality, transverse momentum, and rapidity. The observed particle yields can be effectively described by the available thermal model data, suggesting that these particles participate in the same thermal medium. The experimentally determined particle yields serve as crucial inputs for calculating the coordination number in the QGP and also help to eliminate any influence of freeze-out conditions in the calculation of initial state properties. Additionally, the raw data reveals a notable absence of $\phi$ mesons produced outside of the expected thermal range, particularly in the most peripheral collisions. This anomaly requires further investigation. Lastly, the relative yields of various particles are examined and compared to both theoretical models and prior experiments involving Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. The comparisons reveal similarities in relative yields but also exhibit discrepancies in specific particle production behaviors, particularly in the case of proton relative yields, which exhibit deviations from expected trends. Possible explanations for these discrepancies involve the influence of nucleon-jet correlations. Lastly, the calculated average life spans of the QGP, based on a standard thermal model, range between 4-7 fm. This research significantly enhances our comprehension of the QGP state and its properties, paving the way for enhanced investigations of the QGP state in various collisions. Potential experiments could involve an in-depth examination of the observed anomalies in $\phi$ meson production, particularly in peripheral Xe-Xe collisions, and also investigating the production of other vector mesons in midrapidity and backward rapidity to confirm trends observed in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. Furthermore, the influence of nucleon-jet correlations on proton production could be further explored by conducting experiments at various collision energies. Additionally, the experimentally determined particle yields could be used to investigate the coexistence of the QGP and hadronic matter in a single-particle spectrum. This research greatly expands our knowledge of the two states of matter and their properties and opens up numerous avenues for further investigation. The evolution of parton distribution functions can be accurately modeled using loopy regulator for both singular and quasi-singular QCD equations, allowing for a formal derivation of evolution operators with unknown logarithmic corrections. Incorporating quark masses into the evolution framework via mass-dependent operator methods yields a systematic expansion of parton distribution functions, and thus, their unknown logarithmic corrections. This framework is tested against the poles of Z-factor evolution operators, and we find agreement within the precision of numerical data. Consequently, we derive the logarithmic corrections for all parton flavors. These corrections are necessary for maintaining parton number symmetry in the neutrino-proton DIS cross-section and are crucial for maintaining electroweak gauge boson number conservation. The developed formulae are implemented in the NNLO/MNLO_xPDF code and are scheduled for integration into the xQCD library. The impact of these corrections on parton distribution functions and their influence on various phenomenological parameters such as proton charge radius and form factors are examined. The result shows that higher-order corrections are essential for a satisfactory agreement between data and theory in parton distribution functions. The integrated corrections significantly improve the agreement but still result in small discrepancies. Consequently, higher-twist terms contribute substantially to the proton form factors and parton distribution functions, particularly at low-x and low-Q^2. The input parton distribution functions and their uncertainties need to be adjusted to account for higher-order terms, leading to a substantial change. The same applies to the proton form factors, where higher-order terms result in a change in their values and radial density. The radius of the proton decreases by approximately 5%, while its vector form factor is affected by about 10% or so. The same holds for the vector radiation amplitude A_2 and the Gluck-Reale-Vogt (GRV) PDF. The integration of these parton distribution functions into xQCD will enable the maintenance of parton number symmetry in the neutrino-proton DIS cross-section and electroweak gauge boson number conservation. This study explores and systematizes the effects of three common slip models on the nonlinear behavior of the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. Additionally, we developed a new hydrodynamic model that incorporates all three slip types to study the evolution of liquid coatings on fibers. This model is capable of predicting coating dynamics in the regime where nonlinear effects dominate. Moreover, we analyzed the influence of slip models and surface tension on the system's general behavior, and our findings apply broadly to any given surface slip model. Furthermore, we discovered three different regimes of nonlinear coating dynamics and highlighted the relationship between slip models, coating dynamics, and critical wavelength. This study culminates in a comprehensive comparison of three slip models and provides insight into coating dynamics in three-dimensional systems, ultimately shedding light on the underlying physics of coating dynamics. A key issue in studying galaxy evolution arises from the various methods of deriving star formation rates (SFRs). We compare different methods by using observed data on a sample of 157 galaxies from the MaNGA spectroscopic survey, focusing on a specific spectral line at 2486 angstroms that is not affected by stellar processes and is used as a reference point. By combining data from the MaNGA survey and an earlier study, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of SFR measurements based on spectral analysis, broadband photometry, and a line at 2486 angstroms, allowing us to assess the accuracy of other SFR indicators for the first time. These indicators include broadband photometry and various types of emission lines. We find that SFR estimates based on broadband photometry and certain emission lines are comparable to the 'benchmark' rate derived from the 2486 angstroms line, especially after removing active galactic nucleus influence and considering the contributions of dust particles. Additionally, we find that some single-channel SFR indicators are not only unaffected by active galactic nuclei but also by internal dust particles in galaxies. These indicators include the hydrogen recombination line at 2500 angstroms and the collisionally excited line at 2486 angstroms itself. These characteristics make them particularly suitable for studying galaxies that are difficult to observe up close or have strong active galactic nuclei. On a different note, we find that symmetric derivatives, which are alternative ways of interpreting data related to SFR based on broadband photometry or certain emission lines, can be used with ease and are often comparable to the 'benchmark' rate derived from the 2486 angstroms line. Furthermore, we find that symmetric derivatives can be utilized effectively in low-star-bursting galaxies. Finally, we find that linear and quadratic SFR models derived from line fluxes of different species are equally robust and applicable across various galaxies. On a related note, we find that some SFR models derived from line fluxes of different species are not only unaffected by active galactic nuclei but also by dust particles, including the models based on the MaNGA and the 'benchmark' rate derived from the 2486 angstroms line. These models allow for the effective exploration of the relationships between SFR and other galaxy characteristics, including their stellar masses and radii, as well as various chemical abundances. However, we find that some SFR models derived from line fluxes of different species are not only unaffected by active galactic nuclei but also by dust particles

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a vast array of quantum subgroups of the special linear Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_{N+1}$. The linear representation of these subgroups is studied through the lens of highest weight modules. The authors have devised a method to classify all abelian quantum subgroups, depending on specific parameters, and have identified their regional module structures. The follow-up paper will utilize these findings to pinpoint the diverse collection of type $II$ quantum subgroups. This study presents an innovative approach to synthesizing speech of varied lengths, relying solely on individual speaker-specific data. Our strategy involves selecting median vowels from speakers to create outlier speech, as shorter speech tends to feature more vowels while tone and vowel duration contribute significantly to overall speech length. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness by transforming a male voice into a female voice and altering a neutral voice to sound younger, all based on median vowel characteristics. With its capacity to learn diverse patterns, the system welcomes research collaborations and clinical data contributions from global dermatologists to further refine their diagnoses. To capture the intrinsic variability of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) spectra, a stochastic autoencoder is introduced, designed to learn a noise-corrupted representation of SNe Ia data through intermediate stochastic noise-contrastive estimation. This novel approach diverges from traditional autoencoders by utilizing stochastic encoders and noisy decoders to model the complex, noisy temporal sequences inherent in SNe Ia data. This stochastic autoencoder is applied to a dataset of multiple SNe Ia observations, producing an unsupervised learning method that extracts essential features for intrinsic variability, unaffected by random fluctuations. This purified representation is demonstrated to enhance the separation of SNe Ia phenotypes and remove superficial noise, ultimately enabling the generation of more distinct mock SNe Ia data. Our approach achieves a notable improvement in photon noise reduction, allowing for improved separation of spectroscopic data, up to a classification accuracy of 88.7% using random forests on the purified features. This method contributes towards better utilization of spectroscopic data in improving SNe Ia measurements for cosmology. A related study, 'SNe Ia Spectral Variability: A Deep Learning Approach', is referenced. This related work explores supervised learning with deep neural networks to distinguish between individual SNe Ia spectra, aided by intrinsic variability models captured through our stochastic autoencoders. As a result, improved phenotypic classification accuracy is achieved, up to 89.4% using convolutional neural networks, surpassing traditional methods. This research enables the derivation of well-defined "photographic" parameters, analogous to traditional SNe Ia lightcurve parameters, from spectral temporal series, with potential applications in intrinsic variability modeling and classification. Our work does maintain relationships with these parameters, but omits explicit details to prioritize the focus on temporal series. This research has potential broader impacts due to its versatility in data representation, extending beyond cosmology to various other fields. Additionally, our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenGuanyu/SAE_TDE. This research was funded by the Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), grant number U1738302. Lastly, Chen would like to thank Guangwen Wang for providing the SNEJA dataset. We investigate the process of incorporation of solid particles into thermal plumes under turbulent conditions using a numerical model based on direct numerical simulation. The model distinguishes between the plume's core, where particles are suspended in the fluid, and the plume's periphery, where particles accumulate and form a sediment layer. As the plume rises, particles that collect in the periphery are drawn into the core at the plume's base. Conversely, particles within the core are deposited in the periphery as the plume reaches its maximum height and begins to dissipate. An analysis of incorporation rates, particle sizes, and fluid dynamics within the plume reveals that its dynamics can be described by two non-dimensional numbers: one quantifying the balance between incorporation and fluid dynamics, and another characterizing the accumulation of particles within the plume. Experimental manipulation of these numbers allows us to explore how they influence incorporation rates and particle-size distributions. Our numerical model accurately predicts observations from previous laboratory studies, thereby validating its accuracy and providing a framework for further research. Moreover, our analysis sheds light on the complex interplay between fluid dynamics and solid particle interactions within turbulent plumes. Based on our results, we propose a simplified framework for describing particle incorporation and accumulation that could be applied in a wide range of geological and geophysical settings, such as the formation of volcanic deposits, laccoliths, and igneous intrusions. This framework might also be applicable to contexts involving less turbulent and coherent plumes. An important consideration for further research is the impact of particle stiffness and fracture on incorporation dynamics. Similarly, the influence of biologically significant organisms (e.g., microbes, seeds, and spores) on incorporation dynamics should also be explored. Such organisms often exhibit low to moderate values of particle stiffness. A thorough examination of particle properties and their effects on incorporation dynamics is essential for developing a comprehensive theory that encompasses a diverse range of particle types and turbulent plume configurations. This could lead to a deeper understanding of particle incorporation processes in various geological and geophysical contexts. In order to understand rotating stars, it is essential to study their internal rotation and magnetic field. Studies of solar-type stars have made considerable progress thanks to missions like SOHO/MDI, SDO/AIA and CoRoT/HELIO and research on rotating stars has advanced through projects like asteroseismology and DETHELE. This work focuses on the impact of differential rotation and magnetic field dynamics in low-to-medium activity rotating stars. For this purpose, a revised version of the mean-field theory, taking into account non-uniform rotation and magnetic field dynamo, has been developed. A nonlinear simulation using the mean-field framework has been conducted to investigate how these parameters influence magnetic field predictions. These simulations revealed that varying differential rotation patterns has a significant impact on magnetic field predictions. In particular, incorporating an anti-solar rotation profile in the convection zone results in a weaker magnetic field aligned with the rotation axis. Furthermore, variations in the dynamo $\alpha$-effect sensitivity to magnetic field strength revealed that higher sensitivity produces weaker star magnetic fields and longer magnetic cycle periods. Additionally, eliminating magnetic diffusion in the convective zone leads to shorter magnetic cycle periods. These modifications also result in weaker horizontal magnetic field components and a greater magnetic energy stored in the convective zone. These outcomes indicate that dynamic and spatial variations in internal rotation and magnetic field play important roles in understanding and modelling low-to-medium activity rotating stars. Based on the theoretical period of magnetic cycles, it is possible that some stars observed in projects like DETHELE are actually undergoing magnetic cycles rather than exhibiting constant low activity levels. It is also possible that dynamic variation in the internal magnetic field could produce signatures resembling X-ray flares as seen in projects like CoRoT/HELIO. Further work using asteroseismology and DETHELE is needed to explore the possibility of observing magnetic cycles and dynamic field behaviour in individual stars. Meanwhile, dynamic variation in rotation and internal magnetic field is essential for accurate modelling of low-to-medium activity rotating stars, taking into account variations in angular momentum and energy that drive behaviour like starquakes. Finally, differential rotation and dynamic magnetic field behaviour can result in stored energy that can produce flares and coronal heating exceeding a million times that of the solar average, highlighting the significance of studying dynamic behaviour in low-to-medium activity rotating stars. In the future, it is anticipated that AIA will reveal further evidence of dynamic internal magnetic field behaviour in solar-type stars, corroborated by DETHELE and asteroseismology. Deep learning models built using K-fan transformations - comprising K parallel and identical sub-transformations - often apply equally to signal processing and computer vision. Despite its versatility, current deep learning architectures designed around K-fan structures typically focus on a single type of input data. Therefore, these models are not universally applicable, restricting their use across various disciplines. To address this limitation, we have developed a new multimodal deep framework called the Shared-Rep K-fan Model (SRKM), which can handle multiple types of input data while maintaining a K-fan structure. This innovative model utilizes separate encoders for different input modalities, generates shared representations through an encoder network, and applies a shared decoder to reconstruct the original inputs. Furthermore, we have explored the representation capabilities of the SRKM by pre-training it on various pairs of modalities, resulting in highly generalizable representations. Our experimental findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the SRKM representations on tasks like image denoising and super-resolution, outperforming competing methods. Moreover, we have successfully employed the SRKM representations as a knowledge distillation tool, achieving substantial improvements in performance when compressing K-fan models into smaller architectures. Ultimately, the SRKM represents a significant breakthrough in developing universally applicable deep learning models with K-fan structures, paving the way for future research in deep learning. This work is self-contained and may be tailored to various K-fan ranges, allowing for numerous applications across different fields. The rapid dissemination of unverified information through social media platforms like WhatsApp can contribute to the spread of misinformation. In an effort to address this issue, WhatsApp introduced limitations on the number of people a single user can send certain types of messages to at one time. In this study, we analyze the impact of these restrictions on the dissemination of unverified news among WhatsApp users. We created a stylized model of user behavior to simulate real-world scenarios, applying numerical and experimental methods to evaluate the effects of these restrictions. Our findings suggest that these limitations can significantly reduce the reach of unverified news, but only if the initial group of recipients is limited. We conclude that the usefulness of these restrictions depends on the specific social network structure and the associated costs. Based on our research, we present several open scientific questions related to misinformation spread on social networks. Bloom filters provide efficient memory usage at the cost of precision, suppressing false positives to facilitate quicker system operations. A similar trade-off exists with Bloom and Cuckoo filters, which, to achieve greater memory efficiency, compromise some precision but still suffer from false positives. A more recent alternative, Bloom filters with dependencies, eliminates false positives at the expense of increased computational overhead. A newly developed family of XOR filters, including Chained Hash Filters (CHFs) and Compressed Hash Filters (CHFs), offers superior performance, requiring only one hash function call and offering higher precision and efficiency improvements over existing solutions. A computational scenario involving new element additions in CHFs reveals a trend where, as the number of elements increases, existing solutions experience increased latency while CHFs maintain a constant latency. As an alternative to 7-4 Bloom filters with dependencies, CHFs use fewer memory bits without compromising efficiency or introducing dependencies, also offering superior performance in compression and latency compared to 7-4 CHFs. A proposed family of ultra compact XOR filters, the 6-3 chm family, achieves high precision rates, compresses efficiently, and offers the fastest latency among all solutions. Essential properties of efficient Bloom and Cuckoo filters, such as false positive probabilities and filter sizes, can be deduced from basic CHF properties, including expected bin hits, through statistical analysis. A proposed Chm Filter Designer tool streamlines the process of determining optimal filter configurations for specific false positive probabilities and compression ratios. A comprehensive performance comparison of existing solutions, including a versatile general purpose filter called Generalized Chained Hash Filters (GCHFs), reveals how different configurations of XOR filters can outperform existing solutions in precision, efficiency, and latency. A proposed family of general purpose XOR filters, such as GCHFs, can be used as either efficient, uncompressed Bloom filters or compressed alternatives, also enabling the flexibility to switch between these two forms. To bridge this gap, we demonstrate a practical implementation of a modular temporal pool-based network on the SpiNNaker chip, matching its specifications to neural brain regions capable of learning. We achieve this by using a novel learning rule, 'Liquid Learning', which enables the network to refine its predictions without necessitating neurons to exhibit complex dynamics. The effectiveness of this approach is shown in a sequence learning task where networks, similar to those in the brain, learn to recognize temporal patterns in novel sequences. The results indicate that Liquid Learning not only enables sequence learning, but also converts spiking neural networks into reliable predictors, even in the presence of significant temporal disruption. The detailed exploration of this integration offers a promising pathway for developing robust, biologically feasible artificial intelligence systems. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. However, determining the precision of these expansions is a complex task. This paper presents a verification method that compares the exact solution with an approximation obtained using generalized polynomial chaos expansions. This method acknowledges that exact solutions involving probabilistic variables often cannot be calculated directly due to high-dimensional integrations required, thus developing an auxiliary differential equation to estimate an approximation's accuracy instead. By utilizing this accuracy estimation technique, chaos expansions can be refined and optimized, enabling the detection of approximations that become less accurate as certain parameters change. This method is primarily demonstrated using generalized polynomial chaos expansions in parametric differential algebraic equations, although it can be applied more broadly to other types of equations. Several example applications illustrate the practical use of this verification method. Ultimately, this paper offers an accurate approach to evaluating the reliability of approximation methods that utilize generalized polynomial chaos expansions for analyzing differential equations with uncertain factors. The increasing complexity of modern large-scale systems has led to a significant rise in the use of various adaptive methods that enable partial observation. These methods often rely on the assumption that certain data is readily available and consistent, a condition not met in systems that experience sequential changes, whether anticipated or not. This poses a significant challenge as the system navigates unexpected disruptions, necessitating an updated approach that incorporates non-stationary data dynamics. In response, we present a groundbreaking method that addresses the difficulties posed by changing data dynamics, while also accounting for the limitations of partial observation. This method adapts to varying conditions of observability and system complexity, while providing a clear framework for identifying and isolating significant changes as they occur. A practical application of this method is demonstrated through its use in detecting and resolving changes in a real-world aircraft flight control law. This flight control law was modeled using a highly complex partial state-space approach, with observations restricted to a limited set of sensors, due to hardware limitations, resulting in partial visibility of system states. This makes flight control a particularly demanding adaptive partial observation problem, with critical consequences for safe flight operations. Successful implementation of our method enables the detection and management of changes, while providing essential performance guarantees, ultimately resulting in improved system performance and safety. This work represents the first solution to the fundamental challenges posed by adaptive partial observation in the presence of changing data dynamics, while also addressing the system complexity and limited availability of data, a scenario commonly encountered in real-world applications. A refined hierarchy of Borel Wadge classes is established with the introduction of an efficient classification system. This system builds on the concept of comparison trees, enabling the determination of Borel Wadge classes in a categorization that is both more precise and computationally effective than previous approaches. We demonstrate that any comparison tree of depth n can be evaluated within n times the maximum computational complexity of deciding Borel B_n formulas, and this result is optimal. Furthermore, a related algorithm is presented that determines the lowest Borel Wadge class of a given Borel set with a complexity of O(n^5), marking a significant improvement over previous algorithms requiring exponential time. This development is achieved through a novel decomposition theorem that expresses Borel Wadge classes as finite unions of sets defined by nested conditions of depth n. Additionally, this theorem is applied to analyze the complexity of deciding Borel Wadge classes and finding minimal Borel Wadge embeddings. In contrast to existing research, we find that deciding Borel Wadge classes has a linear complexity for countable Borel sets and identify a specific model where this decision algorithm runs in linear time. Finally, a optimal upper bound of n^4 is found for finding a Borel Wadge embedding between two Borel sets of Wadge class n. This achievement is contingent on the existence of a computable linear ordering of Borel sets. This result marks a significant advancement, improving the previous best result by at least a factor of n. Deep learning models require a considerable amount of data for training, namely a large number of images. Capturing such large datasets typically involves setting up complex infrastructure but then proceeds to remove 95% of the data by eliminating unnecessary image pixels before the learning process begins. A novel approach introduces a mechanism called ClickTrain, which integrates pruning and training phases in a unified end-to-end framework. This method preserves the original structure of the model as it compresses the data, applying pruning to eliminate unnecessary parameters without compromising accuracy. A series of experiments demonstrate that ClickTrain achieves a more efficient model size (10-3 to 10-6 the original) while maintaining high precision on various datasets. Notably, ClickTrain enhances the models' inference speed without affecting their performance on existing datasets, which includes ResNet, MobileNet, Shufflenet, and DenseNet. We examine the relationship between two modal operators, $\Box$ and $\Diamond$, assuming that $\Diamond A$ represents the possibility of formula A being true and $\Box A$ represents the necessity of formula A being true. A connection is established between supersymmetric quantum mechanics and cohomology from algebraic geometry. Specifically, certain cohomologies of a sheaf in complex symplectic geometry are related to the degenerate states of a supersymmetric quantum mechanical system. The first cohomology group corresponds to the ground state and the degenerate states form a non-negative grading based on physical energy levels. The second cohomology group corresponds to physical degenerate states with negative energy. The relationship between cohomology groups in this context generalizes the concept of spectral flow in algebraic geometry. The outcome leads to novel insights in supersymmetric quantum mechanics and reveals a mathematical structure inherent to the framework, potentially expanding the reach of algebraic geometry into physical phenomena. An example is provided using the quartic del Pezzo surface to visualize a supersymmetric quantum mechanical system and its connection to sheaf cohomology. The quantum mechanical Hilbert space is equivalent to the direct sum of cohomologies of stable bundles with positive degree. The ground state forms the first cohomology group, while the degenerate states form the kth cohomology group with k being the degree of the energy levels. The state corresponding to the kth cohomology group has k units of topological winding number, a geometric characteristic that distinguishes it from other degenerate states. The degenerate states with negative energy are found in the kth cohomology group if the energy levels are negative. These results open the door for applying algebraic geometric methods in supersymmetric quantum mechanics to investigate physical phenomena. Actor-critic methods are extensively used for solving complex decision-making problems. However, these models often face challenges related to convergence, such as local optima and overfitting. To address these issues, we introduce a novel actor-critic algorithm that incorporates Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) simulations. This method employs Hamiltonian Dynamics for exploring beyond the limitations of Markov chains, utilizing kinetic energy to simulate trajectories. Furthermore, the introduction of a metacritic layer facilitates the transfer of knowledge across different tasks, effectively enhancing the robustness of the model. To evaluate the performance of our model, we conducted experiments on multiple Atari games, demonstrating its ability to achieve higher rewards and adapt faster across diverse tasks. Additionally, we provide visual representations of trajectories to illustrate the benefits of kinetic energy in identifying action patterns. The integration of HMC technology into actor-critic models offers exciting possibilities for future research and applications. The code for our model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nirmalrajp/ACO.

We develop a novel Bayesian approach to construct uncertainty quantiles for the Q-learning algorithm, a popular off-policy reinforcement learning method. Traditional uncertainty estimation for Q-learning is limited to perturbation-based techniques, which we improve upon by facilitating the incorporation of prior knowledge into uncertainty quantification. Our Bayesian framework, rooted in stochastic optimization, enables the derivation of a quantile function for the first time. As a result, it allows for more accurate pessimism and leads to improved robustness in decision-making, particularly in scenarios involving uncertain and changing environments. Our method, which is amenable to batch processing, can be applied in real-time and adapt to shifting environments. Experimental evaluations, conducted across multiple domains, demonstrate superior performance compared to existing alternatives. Furthermore, prior work's "robustness-games" can be reinterpreted as establishing a performance threshold, achievable through our quantile-based approach. By combining prior knowledge with adaptability, our method enables more informed decision-making and long-term planning. It has practical applications in domains such as public health, automotive systems, and flight control systems. Ultimately, our approach prioritizes accountability and enhances responsibility in the use of reinforcement learning for decision-making. Presence-absence data represents information through a series of binary indicators rather than continuous values. This data form is commonly found in ecological research surveys that list species present at different locations. Various clustering methods have been applied recently to such data using distance measures including the generalized Mahalanobis distance, Mahalanobis distance, Euclidean distance, and Pearson correlation distance. Our study evaluates these clustering methods using simulated datasets and two real-world case studies, comparing their performance in both high and low-dimensional scenarios. Our research indicates that incorporating variance-covariance structure into distance measures yields superior results, particularly in high-dimensional presence-absence data analysis. A linear discriminant analysis followed by a clustering method also demonstrates improved outcomes, albeit slightly, when compared to methods that disregard covariance information. Our findings suggest that treating absence indicators equally can enhance clustering results, while incorporating additional information such as species abundance data may also benefit presence-absence data clustering methods. A comparative summary of clustering methods examined is provided, including their advantages and limitations. Furthermore, potential future research directions based on our observations are suggested. Computed Tomography (CT) is widely employed for detecting internal abnormalities and exploring bodily functions. However, CT scans are often marred by non-ideal external factors like uneven X-ray sources and imperfect detectors. Consequently, reconstructed images from standard filtered backprojection (FBP) algorithms or weighted iterative convex optimizations are typically plagued by artifacts and inaccuracies, making it challenging to accurately identify diverse tissues and external sources. This study introduces a novel non-convex variational framework that simultaneously addresses multiple CT reconstruction challenges, including distortions from varied X-ray energies, external noise, and distinct tissue and external source contributions. To handle these complexities, our proposed framework derives a data fidelity term from a CT measurement model, incorporates Bayesian estimation to filter noise, and distinguishes between tissues and sources through a non-convex regularization term. Our non-convex framework is numerically solved using an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm with a non-convex surrogate function derived from constrained convex optimizations. Our proposed approach is validated through experiments involving numerical phantom simulations and real-world scans from a research CT scanner. Our results demonstrate the capability of our non-convex framework to produce accurate tissue and source maps, as well as enhance image quality by suppressing noise and artifacts. Ultimately, this framework holds promise for various applications, including sensor noise reduction, dual-energy CT, and dynamic function exploration. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is challenging due to the scarcity of labeled data, character variability, and handwriting distinctiveness. The amount of useful information in each handwritten word is relatively low, which complicates training models. Moreover, systems dealing with composite characters (such as 'ch','sh', etc.) are limited in their ability to recognize them. To tackle these challenges, we introduce an innovative method that generates synthetic data from real labels, using a neural network trained on unlabelled data. This new method creates single-shot synthetic data at the character-level, taking into account the complexity of HTR systems' inputs. We compare it to traditional multi-line synthetic data creation and experimentally demonstrate its effectiveness on the datasets, IAM, Rimes, and BCSH, achieving notable improvement in model performance. Notably, our technique outperforms current synthetic data creation approaches, achieving state-of-the-art results on the IAM dataset. In addition, we introduce a novel benchmark for evaluating HTR systems that comprise multiple connected components within a single line. This benchmark, dubbed the Composite Character Recognition (CCR) benchmark, enhances the traditional HTR metric by incorporating a new character error rate that focuses specifically on composite characters. We utilize the CCR benchmark to simulate real-world testing scenarios, where models are faced with composite characters in a single line, and demonstrate its efficacy by achieving a 0.9% character error rate after training on synthetic data created using the single-shot method. This region, nestled near the galaxy's core, is notable for its massive molecular cloud's irregular mass distribution and anisotropic configuration. In this research, a novel mathematical approach is developed to analyze the CMZ's mass setup by comparing the cloud's density patterns in different directions. A completely integrated temperature sensor was designed using a 0.18$\mu$m CMOS process. This temperature sensor operates within a power supply range of 0.6 to 1.8 volts and has a sub-millidegree Celsius resolution. For a voltage supply above 1.8 volts, it uses an external 100k$\Omega$ resistor to measure the temperature of a node connected to a bipolar transistor. This bipolar transistor is connected to a current mirror that converts temperature-dependent base-to-collector voltage into temperature-independent base current. This design offers high accuracy with minimal influence from process variations and voltage supply fluctuations. As a result, it achieves temperature resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius, 1.4 degrees Celsius error margin, and energy per conversion of 1.06 nanojoules. This temperature sensor has both analog and digital output options, with analog output providing analog temperature readings and digital output generating a 10-bit temperature code. Its analog and digital outputs share the same reference point, eliminating the need for an additional voltage regulator. This design accommodates a wide range of operating temperatures, with a top limit of 180 degrees Celsius, and can be used in various applications such as temperature monitoring in harsh environments or as a control parameter in temperature-sensitive operations. It also features two manually controllable adjustment pins that allow users to calibrate temperature readings for precise accuracy. This temperature sensor was tested on a custom evaluation PCB, which can be accessed through a public GitHub repository. Its energy efficiency can be broken down into two parts - analog conversion and digital conversion - with total energy consumption ranging from 1.06 nanojoules to 3.18 nanojoules. These energy figures provide a comprehensive understanding of its operating costs. This temperature sensor was designed with simplicity and a limited number of components to streamline analog conversion process and minimize energy consumption. As a result, it has a simple layout design that can be easily integrated into CMOS process. With its small size and global temperature accuracy, it is an ideal choice for temperature-sensitive applications. Its analog and digital outputs also provide a convenient way to adjust temperature readings for precise accuracy. This temperature sensor offers a convenient and straightforward way to monitor temperature in CMOS processes. The emergence of Primordial Black Holes as potential constituents of dark matter has sparked interest in modelling their formation and impact on the universe. This paper presents a computational tool, PopSyCLE, which predicts the creation of Primordial Black Holes and their influence on the universe's evolution. This tool is validated through a variety states of matter simulation, demonstrating its capability to model a universe dominated by dark matter with a fraction attributed to Primordial Black Holes. The latter's collapse leads to a universe with dark energy, as predicted by the $\Lambda$CDM theory. Therefore, Primordial Black Holes can facilitate a transition from dark matter to dark energy, offering an alternative explanation for the universe's observed evolution. Furthermore, PopSyCLE enables researchers to explore scenarios involving multiple dark matter components and allows for the analysis of observational consequences of Primordial Black Holes, such as their effect on the cosmic microwave background and gravitational waves. In summary, this paper introduces a simulation framework that enables researchers to investigate the universe's evolution influenced by Primordial Black Holes, potentially leading to novel insights and explanations for the universe's observed phenomena. The tool is prepared for further development, enabling the exploration of diverse theoretical scenarios and their comparison with current cosmological data. We explore localized wave patterns, referred to as nanoptera, in two settings: a nonlinear lattice called the woodpile model with weak nonlinear interactions and a granular chain composed of alternating stiff and flexible units. In the weakly nonlinear woodpile system, nanoptera emerge as a superposition of the linear lattice's localized modes, accompanied by a substantial frequency shift. In contrast, the nanoptera of the nonlinear granular chain exhibit a significant gap between its upper and lower frequency bounds, known as the Brillouin gap. Notably, we are able to reproduce the nanoptera's properties of large amplitude and localized behavior, even in the presence of weak nonlinear interactions, which otherwise tends to dissipate energy. Moreover, the nanoptera's stability is assessed through both theoretical and experimental analyses. In the case of the woodpile model, we discover that the nonlinear interactions cause the nanoptera to decay at a rate proportional to the system's dissipation level. In contrast, the nanoptera of the nonlinear granular chain is found to decay exponentially, governed by a characteristic time scale tied to its stiffness. Our findings are further validated by conducting experiments on both the woodpile model and the nonlinear granular chain using advanced laser technology and observational techniques. Ultimately, our investigation sheds light on the intricate dynamics of two distinct systems, shedding new light on the interplay between localization and nonlinear interactions. Additionally, our study explores the feasibility of observing nanoptera in various settings and points to potential avenues for designing materials supporting robust and durable nanoptera. In particular, adjusting the ratio of stiff to flexible units in the granular chain allows us to fine-tune the position of the nanoptera within the frequency spectrum. Consequently, we are able to accurately measure the causes and effects of energy loss in the woodpile model by deliberately introducing disturbances at different points in the system. Ultimately, our research contributes to an in-depth understanding of nanoptera and opens up new paths for investigating and exploiting the unique properties of these localized wave patterns. Additionally, our findings provide new insights into the dynamics of both the woodpile model and the nonlinear granular chain, shedding light on long-standing debates and hypotheses surrounding their behavior. Importantly, we demonstrate the practical feasibility of observing nanoptera in both experiments and simulations, paving the way for future research into the applications of these localized wave patterns. Moreover, our investigation highlights the potential for nanoptera to emerge in a broad range of systems exhibiting weak nonlinear interactions and emphasizes the significance of adjusting parameters to position the nanoptera within the frequency spectrum. In this study, we develop a property-driven approach to ViT development, featuring a self-guided ViT variant that leverages learned intra- and inter-token connections within its transformer framework. By promoting token-to-token interactions through property-based motion dynamics, we enable the ViT to acquire desirable characteristics and, using the CoCo-Vit-61 model as our test case, demonstrate its efficacy on downstream classification tasks after being trained on a relatively small dataset. As a result, the self-guided ViT can produce more accurate predictions on various Vision Transformer models, even when trained using a reduced image size or a dataset that has been deliberately distorted. The proposed architecture is a viable option for creating Vision Transformer models with superior generalization capabilities. By distilling the text realm's steady state, our approach enables the creation of an effective language-specific semantic model. We demonstrate the Steady Creator's potential in various applications such as unsupervised text classification, constrained text generation, and improving translation quality by bridging the gap between text summarization and unsupervised parallel corpora. The proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art models in unsupervised text classification and constrained text generation tasks. Notably, it surpasses the performance of conditioned large-scale language models in these tasks, indicating the significance of targeted semantic models in generating relevant text. We also show that the steady text realm's semantic model enhances the quality of text-based translations, achieving top-ranked results in the TextAdvancement challenge. To facilitate reproducibility, our code and model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/leowooop/steady-creator. Long-term support for this project is available at https://github.com/leowooop/steady-creator/issues. A live demo of the model can be accessed at https://steady-creator.github.io. This study introduces a novel technique for concealing image modifications, ensuring the original content can be fully recovered through reversible operations. A Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) is applied to carry out the concealment, which involves treating network weights as random variables drawing from a prior distribution. When training the BNN, priors evolve into posteriors through Bayes' theorem, ultimately resulting in optimized network weights beneficial for concealment. A derivative-based optimization method is utilized to stochastically estimate BNN weights, yielding significant time reductions compared to traditional optimization methods. Two practical concealment applications, gradient masking and spatial gradient masking, are successfully demonstrated with BNNs, achieving effective results in carrying out these operations. Furthermore, BNN-weighted networks outperform state-of-the-art non-BNN based countermeasures in experiments. This research investigates whether humans can differentiate between linked and unrelated objects moving in different directions, and explores how this ability correlates with processing speeds in the brain. It is discovered that people can efficiently identify dynamic scenarios, completing this task roughly 200 milliseconds faster with linked objects. Employing both behavioral and neuroimaging studies, we examine the underlying mental processes involved, and examine the capability of computational models using optic flow and depth cues to replicate human performance. It is observed that while optic flow models can effectively identify non-linked objects, they struggle with linked objects, suggesting that depth cues play a crucial role. Furthermore, we lastly investigate how minimal human clips, captured using a specialized technique, can provide valuable insights into dynamic scene understanding. Our work offers a new approach to validate computational models using both artificial and real scenes, and demonstrates that linkages between objects significantly impact identification efficiency. It is hoped that this research will contribute valuable insights into dynamic scene understanding and facilitate the development of more effective computational models. Additionally, it is theorized that the minimal clip technique can efficiently gather data, reducing requirements for both hardware and computational resources. Overall, it is concluded that a novel optic flow model, combined with a novel identification strategy, yields the best results among the tested models in replicating human performance. Also, it is shown that linkages between objects substantially impact processing speeds, and that depth cues significantly influence efficient identification. Lastly, it is asserted that shallow neural networks trained on real dynamic scenes, using a novel data preparation method based on minimal clips, can match the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning models. This research offers novel insights into dynamic scene understanding, and potentially enables the development of more agile and efficient artificial intelligence systems capable of navigating complex environments. Predicting climate variables over time is a crucial task that has numerous applications in numerous fields. Despite the efficacy of recurrent neural networks, transformer models have lately shown remarkable potential in handling sequential data with spatial or temporal components. Yet, the distinction between space and time is frequently not acknowledged, leading to poorly optimized performance in climate prediction. In response, a innovative architecture is proposed, specifically the TWCA-Transformer, which integrates cross-attention with a sliding window mechanism to separate and manage temporal and spatial inputs separately. As a result, the model can concentrate on extracting meaningful patterns in each dimension without confusion, resulting in superior performance. The proposed model is then put to the test using a publicly accessible climate dataset, with outstanding results demonstrated, particularly in predicting average winter temperatures. We've expanded on previous research into three-Higgs-doublet models with S_3 symmetry, introducing new models that contain both dark matter and a dark Higgs. These models satisfy the constraints of the electroweak symmetry, including the condition that the oscillation of the dark matter is less than 0.1% per day. Furthermore, we've shown that in one model, the dark matter and dark Higgs are closely related, with the dark Higgs accounting for the majority of the dark matter's mass. We've also identified another model in which the dark matter and dark Higgs behave independently, with the dark Higgs being responsible for a significant component of the dark matter's oscillation. We've presented our findings on our search for these models in particle colliders, specifically in the CMS experiment at the LHC, investigating masses up to 100 GeV for dark matter and 200 GeV for dark Higgs. We've also presented our analysis on the disappearance of leptonically decaying Higgs bosons in this framework. We've found that it's possible to obtain disappearance rates as high as 10^-5 for a certain type of Higgs boson. Additionally, we've found that in the dark matter sector, the rates of leptonic decays are directly proportional to the rates of oscillation. This means that models with minimal oscillation have minimal leptonic decays, whereas models with significant oscillation have significant leptonic decays. We've derived this relationship mathematically. We've also found that in the dark matter sector, the masses of the models are directly related to the oscillation period, with models undergoing oscillation having masses greater than the oscillation mass. This relationship holds for both the singular and double versions of the models. Furthermore, we've found that in the dark matter sector, the couplings of the models are directly proportional to the oscillation, with models undergoing oscillation having stronger couplings. This relationship holds for both the singular and double versions of the models. We've also found that in the dark matter sector, the models with weak couplings are adjacent to the lines of vanishing coupling, with models with medium couplings situated in the center. This information becomes pertinent in the double version of the models, with models undergoing oscillation having neutral couplings that sit on the line of vanishing coupling. It's noteworthy that in the dark matter sector, the models with couplings greater than 10^-2 are far removed from the lines of vanishing coupling

The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis states that any PPT region in a quadrilateral arrangement of pure states remains PPT. We demonstrate that this hypothesis is true for all convex quadrilaterals formed by connecting pure states with maximal entropy along the asymptotic entanglement spectrum. As a result, the PPT hypothesis holds PPTd, which describes a PPT scenario for any local measurement outcome. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis is an integral aspect of the computational complexity of quantum systems, particularly in achieving a dichotomy between PPTd and PPTc. We also explore the related PPT rectangle hypothesis and establish its validity for certain instances, but left many cases undecided. We propose open questions for further investigation. The proof of our main result employs a novel concept called 'good' entropy, enabling a clear division between relevant and irrelevant information in the context of quantum systems. This distinction not only aids in understanding the PPTd and PPTc paradigms but also contributes to broader knowledge of quantum system behavior. Additionally, our work offers a straightforward generalization of the PPT rectangle hypothesis to higher-dimensional systems Arriva. The PPTd and PPTc paradigms have far-reaching implications, extending to scenarios involving random state arrangements and entanglement asymmetry, as we illustrate with specific examples. The integrality of the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis in achieving a dichotomy between PPTd and PPTc paradigms is demonstrated through the analysis of a local complementation operation. We also examine the PPT rectangle hypothesis in conjunction with its complement under local complementation, leading to the concept of PPTrachain, which describes a PPT scenario for any local measurement outcome in a specific chain of interconnected systems. The local complementation operation further enables us to analyze the PPT rectangle hypothesis in a variety of instances and identifies several remaining open questions. The PPTrachain scenario, characterized by a quantum system in a chain arrangement, showcases the complexity of determining the PPT rectangle hypothesis in a definitive manner. The distinct paradigm of PPTrachain illustrates the distinct methods of establishing the PPT rectangle and PPT quadrilateral hypotheses, separate from one another. Furthermore, our work in a complemented scenario demonstrates that the PPT rectangle hypothesis is associated with a fundamental concept in quantum complexity, particularly in understanding the behavior of quantum systems under local measurement. In brain tissue, the regulation of neurotransmitter levels is heavily dependent on the balance between the release and removal of these chemicals by nearby neurons. The rapid exchange creates a complex interplay influencing neural communication precision. We develop a unique mathematical framework, based on an optimization problem incorporating partial differential equations, to examine how neurons manage and exchange substances like neurotransmitters. This novel approach enables us to analyze the spatial distribution of neurons' response to varying levels of excitability and transport capacity. We demonstrate the model's utility by exploring how different transport mechanisms impact substance buildup and the effects of excitability changes through numerical simulations. The model has potential applications in studying neurodegenerative diseases caused by impaired transport and understanding the role of excitability in regulating brain function. Furthermore, this framework can be used to estimate parameters essential for understanding neural communication, such as the rate at which neurons release and absorb substances, by translating it into a related optimal control problem. We illustrate the process of estimating these parameters in a simplified setting. The study provides a foundation for further investigation into the design of experimental treatments aimed at modifying brain activity patterns by influencing excitability and transport processes. The associated data, including PDE implementation, numerical results, and transport estimates, are available for download at the designated repository. In financial markets, the task of identifying meaningful patterns within large market data can be described as an optimization problem, where the target is a small subset of relevant and highly interconnected samples. Building upon the theory of network motifs in social and biological research, we apply this concept to discover hidden patterns within financial time series. Using the BTER dataset, we create a financial network consisting of time-lag interactions and conduct two experiments to demonstrate the feasibility of discovering network motifs. This research contributes to understanding how these patterns interact within the market and has the potential to improve various financial forecasting models by incorporating non-linearity provided by these patterns. The source code for this research study is publicly available on GitHub. In particular, the NeMo-FEVR algorithm, an extension of the FEVR method, is capable of generating network motifs in evolutionary financial datasets. Further details about the feasibility of using network motifs in financial research can be found in a research note previously published by the author. A related JSE paper explores the statistical properties of these patterns in more detail. This research is based on a dissertation thesis that examines the reproducibility of these patterns, where we conduct two experiments using different algorithms - FEVR and FeVR+NM - on distinct financial datasets. A key outcome of this research reveals that the FeVR+NM algorithm is capable of generating significant and persistent results. In summary, this research, specifically NeMo, demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of using network motifs to discover meaningful patterns within financial data. A related project, Fisher, is dedicated to testing the hypothesis that these patterns are not randomly generated.
